# Ostler

> Ostler is an open-source MCP browser for AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. It reads, researches and acts in a real Chrome, and checks its own work: research answers cite only pages it actually read, with every quote verified; forms are filled in one call with every value read back; and Qdrant remembers what worked.

Ostler is one local Rust binary (Apache-2.0) that runs Chrome and speaks MCP over stdio to coding agents and A2A over HTTP to other agents. It has no LLM inside, no cloud browser and no anti-bot evasion. Status: v0.2, early (development source; no tagged release yet); tested against real Chrome and Qdrant on local fixtures, not yet benchmarked on the open web.

Key facts:

- Install: `pip install ostler-mcp` (or `uvx --from ostler-mcp ostler serve`), then `ostler start` (connects every AI app it finds) or `ostler setup claude --apply` (Claude Code); or see the agents page for Codex, Cursor and VS Code.
- Other ways to install (v0.2.0): the install script for macOS and Linux (https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/install.sh), Claude Desktop `.mcpb` (macOS), the VS Code extension on Open VSX (https://open-vsx.org/extension/inamdarmihir/ostler), and `cargo install --git https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler ostler` from source. Windows (x86_64, experimental) and a Docker image (`ghcr.io/inamdarmihir/ostler`) arrive in v0.2.1. Not published yet: the VS Code Marketplace, Homebrew, npm and crates.io.
- Requirements: Chrome or Chromium; Python 3.8+ for pip (no Rust); Rust 1.89+ only for the from-source install.
- Evidence: local fixtures; a five-task scripted comparison with Playwright MCP and Chrome DevTools MCP; seven live public practice pages. Not yet measured on the open web.
- Browsing: a general MCP browser in a real Chrome. 16 core tools: navigate, snapshot, read, click, type, tabs, screenshots and `look` (numbered click targets). Log in once with `--profile-dir`; CAPTCHAs are handed to a person, never solved.
- Research: `read` returns the best passages for a query; `cite` marks a quote VERIFIED only if its words are on a page read this session; `evidence` lists citations and the pages that could not be read (paywall, bot wall, robots.txt).
- Forms: `form_fill` fills a whole form in one call and reads every value back; 3 tool calls instead of 22 on a 20-field form (same engine, one call per field; scripted, model-free, local fixtures).
- Memory: optional, in Qdrant or an encrypted local file; stores facts you save and per-site playbooks (structure, not values). Secret-looking values are refused; detection is heuristic. Tool output goes to your MCP client and, through it, to that client's model provider.
- Safety: page text is fenced as untrusted, a domain allowlist holds every request, CAPTCHAs are handed to a person.


---

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/get-started.html

# Getting started (no programming needed)

Ostler lets an AI assistant (Claude, Cursor, Codex) use a real web browser on your computer: read pages, research a topic with sources it actually read, and fill in web forms. You do **not** need Rust, Node or any code. Back to the [README](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/README.md).

**Status:** early (v0.2). v0.2.0 is released, so the download steps below work (macOS and Linux; Windows and Docker arrive in the next release, experimental). The VS Code Marketplace, crates.io and npm are not published yet ([INSTALL](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/INSTALL.md)).

## What you need

- A Mac or Linux computer. Windows and Docker are not released yet (planned v0.2.1, experimental, with known gaps listed in [COMPATIBILITY](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/COMPATIBILITY.md#known-windows-and-docker-gaps-v020-source)).
- **Google Chrome** ([download](https://www.google.com/chrome/)).
- An AI app that supports MCP: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf or Codex.

## Path A: Claude Desktop on a Mac (one double-click)

1. Open the [latest release](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/releases/latest) and download the `.mcpb` file for your Mac (`aarch64` = Apple silicon M1 or newer, `x86_64` = Intel).
2. Double-click it. Claude Desktop shows an install prompt; click **Install**.
3. Start a chat and ask: *"Open https://example.com and tell me what the page says."*

## Path B: any supported app, one command

Open **Terminal** (Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal) and paste:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/install.sh | sh
ostler start
```

`ostler start` finds the AI apps on your computer, connects Ostler to each one, checks that Chrome is there, and tells you what to restart. It backs up any file it changes, keeps your other settings, and is safe to run twice. To undo: `ostler install --client <name> --uninstall` (`ostler install --list` shows the names).

Then **quit and reopen your AI app**.

## Path C: VS Code, Cursor or Windsurf extension

Search the extensions panel for **Ostler** (Open VSX for Cursor and Windsurf; the VS Code Marketplace listing is not published yet), install it, and Ostler appears as an MCP server. No terminal. It uses an `ostler` already on your PATH, or downloads the matching release once and checks its checksum. Commands: *Ostler: Check setup*, *Ostler: Sign in to a website*. Source: [editors/vscode](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/tree/main/editors/vscode).

## Path D: Python (`pip` or `uvx`)

```sh
pip install ostler-mcp        # adds the `ostler` command (use pipx or `uv tool install` to keep it isolated)
ostler start
```

Or with no install step, in any MCP client's config: command `uvx`, arguments `["--from", "ostler-mcp", "ostler", "serve"]`. The package is the same Rust program inside a Python wheel (no Python code, nothing downloaded at run time). The name is `ostler-mcp` because `ostler` on PyPI is a different project.

## Path E: one-click links for Cursor and VS Code

After installing the `ostler` command (Path B, first line), these links add it to the app:

- [Add to Cursor](https://cursor.com/install-mcp?name=ostler&config=eyJjb21tYW5kIjoib3N0bGVyIiwiYXJncyI6WyJzZXJ2ZSJdfQ==)
- [Add to VS Code](https://insiders.vscode.dev/redirect/mcp/install?name=ostler&config=%7B%22name%22%3A%22ostler%22%2C%22command%22%3A%22ostler%22%2C%22args%22%3A%5B%22serve%22%5D%7D)

They assume `ostler` is on your `PATH`; `ostler start` does not need that. The link formats follow the apps' published install-link schemes but have not been tested here.

## Ready-made prompts

Apps that show MCP prompts (Claude Desktop lists them under the **+** menu) offer five from Ostler: summarize a page, research with checked sources, fill in a form (review before sending), check my web page, compare pages. Pick one, fill in the blank, send.

## Signing in to a website

For tasks behind a login, sign in once yourself:

```sh
ostler login https://example.com/login
```

A Chrome window opens. Sign in, then press Enter in Terminal. Then connect Ostler with that saved session: `ostler install --client claude-desktop -- --profile-dir ~/.ostler/profile`. Anyone who can read that folder can use your sign-in, so use it on your own computer only.

## Things to ask

- "Open this page and summarize it: <link>"
- "Research <topic>. Only use pages you actually read, and check every quote against the page."
- "Fill in the contact form on <link> with my name and email, then show me what you entered before submitting."
- "Check that the login page on my site still works after my change."

For a safe practice page, run `ostler fixtures` and ask the assistant to fill in the form at http://127.0.0.1:8787/dependent.html. Nothing real is submitted.

## Extra caution

`ostler start --cautious` connects Ostler so page requests that change things (form posts and similar) are blocked unless the assistant uses its confirmed submit step. It is stricter than normal and can also stop some sign-ins or buttons. Run `ostler start` again without the flag to go back.

## What the messages mean

| you see | meaning |
|---|---|
| `VERIFIED` / `NOT VERIFIED` | the quoted words were (or were not) found on a page the assistant actually read. It proves the words are there, not that they are true |
| `NOT READ` | the assistant cited a page it never opened |
| gaps in `evidence` | pages it could not read (paywall, bot check, blocked by the site's robots.txt, error) |
| `CHALLENGE:` | the site showed a CAPTCHA or "are you human" check. Ostler does not solve these |
| `UNMATCHED key` | a detail you gave matches no field on the form, so nothing was guessed |
| `NOT ACCEPTED` | the site rejected the form and says why |

## Good to know

- Ostler uses its own Chrome window, hidden by default. To sign in to a site once and reuse it, or to solve a CAPTCHA yourself, see [Troubleshooting](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/troubleshooting.html).
- Ostler does not solve CAPTCHAs and does not submit real forms unless you ask the assistant to.
- Your AI app may send what it reads to its own model provider. Ostler itself sends pages nowhere.

## If something goes wrong

Run `ostler doctor`. Every failing check prints the exact fix. More in [Troubleshooting](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/troubleshooting.html).


---

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/quickstart.html

# Quickstart

Install Ostler, check that it can drive Chrome, connect your agent, and try it on a demo page: read and cite a source, or fill a form. About five minutes.

> [!NOTE]
> **Status: v0.2, early.** Ostler is tested against real Chrome and a real Qdrant server, but only on local fixtures, not the open web. A [design review](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/review.html) found real flaws and lists them openly with a fix order. Read [what that means](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/economics.html#6-what-can-go-wrong) before relying on it.

## 1. Install

You need **Chrome or Chromium** (Ostler drives a real browser) and Python 3.8+ (no Rust needed).

```sh
pip install ostler-mcp
```

No Python? Use the install script (macOS and Linux): `curl -fsSL https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/install.sh | sh`. With Rust 1.89+ you can build from source: `cargo install --git https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler ostler`. Every option, and what is not published yet (npm, crates.io, Homebrew), is on the [Install](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/install.html) page.

## 2. Check it works

```sh
ostler doctor
```

`ostler doctor` launches Chrome, round-trips a page and, if you configured Qdrant, prints a memory report (sealing, key location, where embeddings are computed, isolation, transport) and checks that Qdrant is reachable. When something is wrong it prints the command that fixes it; `ostler doctor --fix` applies the safe ones (creating the config directory). With no config at all, memory is in-process for the session and nothing needs Qdrant or a key. See [Troubleshooting](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/troubleshooting.html) if it does not pass.

## 3. Connect your agent

```sh
ostler install --client claude-code      # or claude-desktop | cursor | vscode | windsurf | codex
```

That writes the entry into the client's config file with the binary's absolute path: it backs the file up first, keeps your other servers, refuses a malformed file and prints what changed (`--dry-run` previews, `--uninstall` removes). `ostler install --list` shows every client. To only print a snippet instead, use `ostler setup <client>`. Prefer your own Chrome window? See "Use your own Chrome" on the [Install](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/install.html) page. Details for every client are in [Use with your agent](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/agents.html).

After installing or rebuilding `ostler`, reconnect the MCP client (Claude Code: `/mcp`; others: restart it) so it starts the new binary.

## 4. Try the demo

```sh
ostler fixtures        # serves synthetic test pages at http://127.0.0.1:8787
```

Pick one. Nothing real is read or submitted; these are bundled test pages.

**Research with a checked quote.** Ask your agent:

> *Read http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html. Who designed the Kestrel Lock and when did it open? Cite every claim with `cite` and call `evidence` before answering.*

Ostler reads the page, accepts a quote that is on it, refuses one that is not, and lists any page it could not read. The full walk-through, with unedited output, is in [Research with checked citations](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/research-with-citations.html).

**Fill a form.** Ask your agent:

> *Open http://127.0.0.1:8787/dependent.html and fill in the shipping form for Ada Lovelace in Germany, Bavaria.*

Ostler fills Country, watches State load, reads every value back, and reports what the page said.

## What the agent sees

### Research

Unedited output from the bundled research pages (`ostler serve --tools research`), captured 2026-11-06. The `<page_content untrusted="true">` tags mark text that came from the page.

```text
> cite {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html", "quote": "opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta Ilves"}
VERIFIED [1] <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html</page_content> (read 2026-11-06T16:01:32Z, sha256:9f602117)
<page_content untrusted="true">opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta Ilves</page_content>
Check it yourself (best effort): http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html#:~:text=opened%20in%201887%20and%20was%20designed%20by%20Marta%20Ilves

> cite {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html", "quote": "Tomas Reyes designed the Kestrel Lock in 1887"}
NOT VERIFIED: these words are not on <page_content untrusted="true">The Kestrel Lock</page_content>. Do not state this claim as sourced; quote the page's own words, not a summary.
Closest text on the page (similarity 0.48): <page_content untrusted="true">The Kestrel Lock The Kestrel Lock is a double</page_content>
```

`cite` proves the words are on the page, not that the claim is true.

### A form

Real output from the bundled fixtures (`ostler serve --tools forms`), with the `<page_content>` fences left out and one `<-` note added. *State* is disabled until *Country* is chosen.

```text
> form_inspect
form [e2] fingerprint=07efd5b3061187a1
  e3 text    "Recipient"      [required]
  e4 select  "Country"        [required] options: Choose… | United States | Germany | India
  e5 select  "State / region" [required, disabled] options: (Choose a country first)
  e6 text    "City"
  e7 submit  "Ship it"

> form_fill {"Country": "Germany", "State": "Bavaria", "Email": "ada@example.com"}
Filled 2/3.
verified: "Country", "State / region"      <- State's options loaded after Country changed
  UNMATCHED key "Email": no field on the page matches this key
Still empty and required:
  e3 "Recipient"

> form_submit
NOT ACCEPTED: the page reported problems.
  e3 "Recipient": "Please fill in this field."
```

A key that matches nothing is reported, not guessed. A rejected submit says why, in the page's words. More on how this works in [Forms and verification](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/forms.html).

## Things to ask your agent

- "Find out what this page says about the rate limit and quote the sentence. Say so if you could not read it." (`read`, `cite`, `evidence`)
- "Compare the pricing on these three pages and tell me what you could not check." (`open_many`, `evidence`)
- "Open this web app, click through the signup flow and tell me what breaks." (`navigate`, `click`, `look`)
- "Fill in the contact form on this page with my details." (after `memory_remember` of your name and email, or with `--learn`)
- "Sign up for the newsletter on example.com, but ask me before you submit." (`--require-confirm-submit`)
- "This form has a date picker and a country dropdown: fill it and tell me anything you couldn't verify."
- "What's blocking this page?" (`look` shows numbered click targets; a CAPTCHA is reported, not bypassed)

## Optional: memory

Browsing, reading, citing and form filling need no account and no key (only `search` needs a provider). Memory is separate and optional:

```sh
ostler init                                   # saves your Qdrant URL, key and privacy choices (sealing, embeddings, retention); tests the connection
ostler install --client claude-code -- --learn --lean # re-register with memory flags
```

See [Memory and privacy](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/memory.html) for exactly what is stored and what is hidden.

## Next steps

- [Use with your agent](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/agents.html): Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, anything else.
- [Tools reference](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/tools.html): all 32 tools and their parameters.
- [Security model](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/security.html): the allowlist, uploads, dialogs, CAPTCHAs.

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/install.html

# Install

Ostler is a single Rust binary, `ostler`, that launches and drives Chrome. You need **Chrome or Chromium** installed. Pick one way to get the binary. v0.2.0 is released; the table says what is live today.

| how | command | needs |
|---|---|---|
| **Python** ([PyPI: ostler-mcp](https://pypi.org/project/ostler-mcp/)), **live** | `pip install ostler-mcp`, or `uvx --from ostler-mcp ostler serve` | Python 3.8+ or uv; the wheel carries the binary |
| Prebuilt binary, **live** | `curl -fsSL https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/install.sh \| sh`, then `ostler start` | nothing else; macOS and Linux |
| Claude Desktop (Mac), **live** | download the `.mcpb` from the [release](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/releases/latest) and double-click it | nothing else |
| **VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf**, **live on Open VSX** ([Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/extension/inamdarmihir/ostler)) | install the **Ostler** extension. The VS Code Marketplace listing is not published yet. | the editor; no terminal |
| **From source**, works anywhere | `cargo install --git https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler ostler` | Rust 1.89+, a minute or two to compile |
| Docker, next release (v0.2.1) | `docker run -i --rm ghcr.io/inamdarmihir/ostler` | Docker; bundles Chromium, runs as a non-root user |
| Windows (x86_64), next release (v0.2.1), experimental | download `ostler-v<version>-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.tar.gz` from the release, or `pip install ostler-mcp` | Chrome or Edge installed |
| Homebrew, not working yet | `brew install inamdarmihir/ostler/ostler` | the tap is not being updated yet |
| npm / `npx`, not published yet | `npx -y ostler doctor` | Node 18+ |
| crates.io, not published yet | `cargo install ostler` or `cargo binstall ostler` | Rust |

> [!NOTE]
> **Availability (v0.2.0):** the rows marked live work today. The others are not published yet, so their pages show "not found"; PyPI and the install script always work. Release process: [RELEASING.md](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/RELEASING.md). Not a developer? Start with [Getting started, no programming needed](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/get-started.html).

## Where Ostler is listed

- Source and releases: [GitHub](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler) and [releases](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/releases)
- Python: [PyPI, `ostler-mcp`](https://pypi.org/project/ostler-mcp/) (the name `ostler` on PyPI is a different project)
- Editors: [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/extension/inamdarmihir/ostler) for Cursor, Windsurf and other forks (the VS Code Marketplace listing is not published yet)
- Not published yet: npm (`ostler`), crates.io (`ostler`), the Homebrew tap and the Docker image (`ghcr.io/inamdarmihir/ostler`, next release)

## Verify

```sh
ostler doctor        # Chrome launches? Memory report; Qdrant reachable? Every failing check prints the command that fixes it
ostler doctor --fix  # apply only the safe fixes: create the config directory, chmod 600 an open key file
```

`ostler doctor` explains launch failures (sandbox or root problems, a profile already in use, missing libraries, Chrome not installed) with a concrete command for each. `--fix` never creates keys, installs software, edits client configs or touches the network.

## Connect your agent

Easiest: `ostler start` finds the AI apps on your computer and connects Ostler to each. Or pick one:

```sh
ostler install --list                  # clients and their config files
ostler install --client claude-code    # or claude-desktop | cursor | vscode | windsurf | codex
```

This edits the client's config file for you: it refuses a file that is not valid JSON/TOML, makes a backup first, keeps your other servers and prints exactly what changed. Re-running it changes nothing; `--dry-run` previews and `--uninstall` removes the entry. Nothing else needs configuring: with no config at all, memory is in-process for the session and no Qdrant or key is involved.

## Use your own Chrome (optional)

Start Chrome yourself with a debugging port on loopback and a dedicated profile, then point Ostler at it:

```sh
"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --remote-debugging-port=9222 --remote-debugging-address=127.0.0.1 --user-data-dir=$HOME/.ostler/chrome-profile
ostler doctor --cdp-url http://127.0.0.1:9222
ostler install --client claude-code -- --cdp-url http://127.0.0.1:9222
```

Only loopback is accepted. Ostler never opens the port for you, works in its own tab and leaves your browser running. While the port is open any local program can drive that Chrome, so use a dedicated profile.

## Platforms

- **macOS:** tested locally.
- **Linux:** tested in CI. In containers or as root you may need `OSTLER_NO_SANDBOX=1`, plus a larger `/dev/shm` (`--shm-size=1g`) for Chrome. See [Troubleshooting](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/troubleshooting.html).
- **Windows (x86_64):** builds and runs its test suite in CI; ships from the next release (v0.2.1). Experimental, with no day-to-day use yet. Known gaps in v0.2.0 source: config falls back to a `.config` folder in the current directory (set `OSTLER_CONFIG`), Chrome is found only under `Program Files` (set `OSTLER_CHROME` for Edge or a per-user Chrome), there is no PowerShell installer and no Windows wheel.
- **Docker (linux/amd64, linux/arm64):** ships from the next release (v0.2.1). Headless only, so `wait_for_human` cannot show a window; saved logins need a writable volume for uid 10001.
- **Browser:** Chrome or Chromium only. If Chrome is in a non-standard place, set `OSTLER_CHROME=/path/to/chrome` or pass `--chrome-path`.

## Update

Rerun the same install command. `install.sh` replaces the binary in place. Then reconnect your MCP client (Claude Code: `/mcp`; others: restart it) so it starts the new binary.

## Uninstall

Run `ostler install --client <name> --uninstall` for each client you registered (it keeps your other servers and backs the file up). Delete the `ostler` binary (`~/.local/bin/ostler`, or `~/.cargo/bin/ostler`), and `~/.config/ostler` and `~/.cache/ostler` if you want the settings and the `npx` download gone.

Memory lives in your Qdrant, not on disk here. `ostler memory wipe --yes` erases it, so run that first if you want it gone.

## What gets written to disk

By default, nothing apart from the binary and, if you run `ostler init`, the config file `~/.config/ostler/config.toml` (owner-only permissions). With sealed memory, a key file `memory.key` next to the config. Chrome uses a throwaway profile unless you pass `--profile-dir`. Ostler sends no telemetry.

## The prebuilt installer

`install.sh` is served from this site and verifies a checksum before installing; on a mismatch it installs nothing and runs nothing. It installs to `~/.local/bin` by default (`OSTLER_INSTALL_DIR` changes that, `OSTLER_VERSION` pins a version) and never edits your shell profile or your agent's config. You can read the script first: [install.sh](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/install.sh).


---

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/agents.html

# Use with your agent

Ostler is an MCP server over stdio. Any MCP client can launch it. `ostler setup <client>` prints the exact config, using this binary's **absolute path**. That avoids "command not found" when an app's `PATH` differs from your shell's.

| client | command | result |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `ostler setup claude --apply` | runs `claude mcp add` for you |
| Codex | `ostler setup codex` | prints the block for `~/.codex/config.toml` |
| Cursor | `ostler setup cursor` | prints JSON for `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
| VS Code | `ostler setup vscode` | prints JSON for `.vscode/mcp.json` |
| anything else | `ostler setup json` | generic `mcpServers` JSON |

Only Claude Code is applied automatically. Other clients' files are never modified: you paste or merge the printed snippet. Extra `serve` flags go after `--`:

```sh
ostler setup claude --apply -- --lean --tools forms
```

> [!NOTE]
> Client config formats change between releases. If one of these does not load, check that client's current MCP documentation. The server itself only needs `ostler serve` on stdio.

## Claude Code

```sh
ostler setup claude --apply
# manual equivalent:
claude mcp add ostler -- ostler serve
```

Reconnect with `/mcp` after installing or rebuilding.

## Codex

```sh
ostler setup codex
```

Prints a block for `~/.codex/config.toml`. Paste or merge it:

```toml
[mcp_servers.ostler]
command = "/absolute/path/to/ostler"
args = ["serve"]
```

## Cursor

```sh
ostler setup cursor
```

Prints JSON for `~/.cursor/mcp.json` (or `.cursor/mcp.json` in a project):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ostler": {
      "command": "/absolute/path/to/ostler",
      "args": ["serve"]
    }
  }
}
```

## VS Code

Easiest: install the **Ostler** extension from [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/extension/inamdarmihir/ostler) (Cursor, Windsurf and other forks; the VS Code Marketplace listing is not published yet). It registers Ostler as an MCP server, uses an `ostler` on your PATH or downloads and checks the release once, and adds *Ostler: Check setup* and *Ostler: Sign in to a website*. Source: [editors/vscode](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/tree/main/editors/vscode).

Or by hand:

```sh
ostler setup vscode
```

Prints JSON for `.vscode/mcp.json`. VS Code uses a `servers` key and an explicit transport type:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "ostler": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "/absolute/path/to/ostler",
      "args": ["serve"]
    }
  }
}
```

## With uvx or pip (no Rust)

Any MCP client can launch Ostler from the Python package [`ostler-mcp`](https://pypi.org/project/ostler-mcp/) (it carries the same binary):

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "ostler": { "command": "uvx", "args": ["--from", "ostler-mcp", "ostler", "serve"] } } }
```

`pip install ostler-mcp` instead puts the `ostler` command on your PATH. Use `pipx` or `uv tool install` to keep it isolated.

## Any other MCP client

```sh
ostler setup json
```

prints the common `mcpServers` shape. The only requirement is that the client starts `ostler serve` and speaks MCP over stdio. `ostler serve` should print one `ready` line on stderr and wait; stdout carries only MCP messages.

Building your own agent in Python? See [LangChain, LlamaIndex and AutoGen](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/frameworks.html) for tested code. Keep one Ostler session open for the whole task, or `cite` will not see what `read` fetched.

## A good agent workflow

For research with citations:

1. `search` (or start from known URLs), then `open_many` with a `query` to read the best passages of up to 10 pages.
2. `read` with a `query` to go deeper on one page; follow `links` or `extract` tables and lists.
3. `cite` every quote you intend to use. Only `VERIFIED` quotes go in the answer.
4. `evidence` before answering: it lists the verified citations and the pages that could not be read, which the answer should name as gaps.

A prompt that works: *"Research X. Cite every claim with `cite`; call `evidence` before answering and list what you could not read."*

For reading or testing a page:

1. `navigate` opens the page and lists its interactive elements; `snapshot` returns the page as text (pass a heading's ref to read one section).
2. `look` returns a screenshot with numbered click targets, which helps when a cookie banner or modal is in the way.
3. `click`, `type`, `press` and `wait_for` act on the page; `screenshot` captures the result. Page text arrives fenced as untrusted, so instructions inside a page are data, not commands.

For forms:

1. `navigate` returns the page's interactive elements.
2. `form_inspect` returns typed fields and shows what memory knows about this form.
3. `form_fill` with `{label: value}` for what you know; add `auto: "required"` to fill the rest from memory.
4. `form_submit`, then read the status: *Submitted*, *Advanced* (next step: repeat 2 to 4), or *NOT ACCEPTED* with the page's validation messages.

`ostler inspect <url>` prints the form model as JSON for debugging.

## Control what the agent sees and can do

| flag | effect |
|---|---|
| `--tools core\|forms\|all` | which tools the agent sees (12, 16 or 21). Fewer tools means less schema in every turn |
| `--allow-domain example.com` (repeatable) | only that domain and subdomains, every request and WebSockets included; `example.com:8443` pins a port |
| `--require-confirm-submit` | `form_submit` fails unless the agent passes `confirm=true`, so a human can approve |
| `--upload-dir DIR` (repeatable) | file fields may be filled from this directory; without it uploads are refused |
| `--block-private-networks` | with no allowlist, refuse loopback, private, metadata and internal hosts |
| `--accept-dialogs` | answer the page's `confirm()` and `prompt()` with OK; they are dismissed by default |
| `--lean` | lower memory; no images, fonts or media |
| `--profile-dir DIR` | persistent Chrome profile (keeps logins); one profile per server |
| `--headed` | visible browser, for watching it work and for `wait_for_human` |
| `--learn` | save non-sensitive values typed after an accepted submit (off by default) |

The full flag list is on the [Configuration and CLI](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/configuration.html) page, and the reasoning is in the [Security model](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/security.html).

## Tabs share one browser context

Cookies and logins carry across tabs. The `context` tool is a small key/value notepad that every tab and every later call can read, for things like "applicant = Ada, order id = 4471". It survives a browser restart. Popups arrive as tabs under the same domain policy.

## Other agents: A2A

If another agent, rather than a coding agent, should hand Ostler a form, use [A2A](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/a2a.html) instead of MCP.

## Use the Chrome you already have

Ostler can drive a Chrome you started yourself, so you keep your own window and sessions:

1. Start Chrome with a debugging port on loopback and a dedicated profile (Chrome ignores the flag on its default profile; you start this, Ostler never opens the port for you):
   - macOS: `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --remote-debugging-port=9222 --remote-debugging-address=127.0.0.1 --user-data-dir=$HOME/.ostler/chrome-profile`
   - Linux: `google-chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --remote-debugging-address=127.0.0.1 --user-data-dir=$HOME/.ostler/chrome-profile`
2. Check it: `ostler doctor --cdp-url http://127.0.0.1:9222` (opens one blank tab, closes it).
3. Register it: `ostler install --client claude-code -- --cdp-url http://127.0.0.1:9222`.

The one-prompt flow: tell your agent "start Chrome with the command above, then run `ostler doctor --cdp-url http://127.0.0.1:9222`", then install as in step 3.

Safety: only loopback URLs are accepted (a DevTools port has no authentication: anything that can reach it controls the browser, including every logged-in site), the URL is checked when `serve` starts, Ostler works in a tab of its own and closes only that tab on exit, and your browser keeps running. While the port is open, any local program can drive that Chrome, so use a dedicated profile and close it when done. `--cdp-url` conflicts with `--profile-dir`, is refused in A2A mode, and `--allow-domain` then relies on request interception without Chrome's DNS pinning.


---

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/frameworks.html

# Use Ostler from LangChain, LlamaIndex and AutoGen

Ostler is an MCP server, so any agent framework with an MCP adapter can use its browser, research and form tools. This page shows the three popular Python frameworks, with the code that was run and the output it produced.

**What was tested, and what was not.** Each snippet below was run against Ostler 0.2.0 and the bundled demo page (`ostler fixtures`): the adapter connects over stdio, loads the tools, and calls `read` then `cite` directly. **No language model was in the loop**, so the step that hands the tools to an agent is shown as documented usage and marked as not run.

## The one rule: keep one session open

`cite` only accepts a quote from a page that `read` fetched **in the same Ostler session**. A session is one running Ostler process. Adapters differ in whether they keep it:

| framework | default behaviour | what to do |
|---|---|---|
| LangChain (`langchain-mcp-adapters`) | `client.get_tools()` starts a new Ostler process per tool call, so `cite` returns `NOT READ` | open `client.session("ostler")` and use `load_mcp_tools(session)` |
| LlamaIndex (`llama-index-tools-mcp`) | `BasicMCPClient` starts a new process per call, so `cite` returns `NOT READ` | open an `mcp.ClientSession` yourself and pass it to `McpToolSpec` |
| AutoGen (`autogen-ext[mcp]`) | `McpWorkbench` as a context manager keeps one session | use `async with McpWorkbench(params)` |

Both failures were observed, not assumed: the `NOT READ` reply is `NOT READ: <url> was not read in this session ... call read first`. It is Ostler refusing to certify a quote from a page it did not read in that session, which is the point of `cite`. Run the agent inside the `async with` block; when the block exits, the Ostler process and its Chrome end and the read history is gone.

Every example assumes `ostler` is on your `PATH` (see [install](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/install.html)) and the demo pages are being served with `ostler fixtures`. `--tools research` pins the 21 research-profile tools; use `--tools all` for all 30 ([profiles](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/tools.html)).

## LangChain

```sh
pip install langchain-mcp-adapters      # tested: 0.3.2, with mcp 1.30.0
```

```python
import asyncio
from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient
from langchain_mcp_adapters.tools import load_mcp_tools

URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html"
client = MultiServerMCPClient({"ostler": {"transport": "stdio", "command": "ostler",
                                          "args": ["serve", "--tools", "research"]}})

async def main():
    async with client.session("ostler") as session:  # one session = one Ostler process
        tools = {t.name: t for t in await load_mcp_tools(session)}
        print("loaded:", len(tools), list(tools)[:8])
        await tools["read"].ainvoke({"url": URL})
        for quote in ["It opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta Ilves",
                      "Tomas Reyes designed the Kestrel Lock in 1887"]:
            r = await tools["cite"].ainvoke({"url": URL, "quote": quote})
            print(r[0]["text"][:90].replace("\n", " "))

asyncio.run(main())
```

Output (the second quote is a decoy that is not on the page):

```
loaded: 21 ['navigate', 'snapshot', 'read', 'click', 'type', 'press', 'hover', 'scroll']
VERIFIED [1] <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-l
NOT VERIFIED: these words are not on <page_content untrusted="true">The Kestrel Lock</page
```

Tool results come back as a list of content blocks, so the text is `r[0]["text"]`. To hand the tools to an agent, keep the agent call inside the same `async with` block. **Not run** (no model available here; `langchain` and a model package are extra installs):

```python
from langchain.agents import create_agent
async with client.session("ostler") as session:
    agent = create_agent("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", await load_mcp_tools(session))
    await agent.ainvoke({"messages": "Who designed the Kestrel Lock? Cite the exact quote."})
```

## LlamaIndex

```sh
pip install llama-index-tools-mcp       # tested: 0.6.0, with mcp 2.3.0
```

```python
import asyncio
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client
from llama_index.tools.mcp import McpToolSpec

URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html"
SERVER = StdioServerParameters(command="ostler", args=["serve", "--tools", "research"])

async def main():
    async with stdio_client(SERVER) as (r, w), ClientSession(r, w) as session:  # one Ostler process
        await session.initialize()
        tools = {t.metadata.name: t for t in await McpToolSpec(session).to_tool_list_async()}
        print("loaded:", len(tools), list(tools)[:8])
        await tools["read"].acall(url=URL)
        for quote in ["It opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta Ilves",
                      "Tomas Reyes designed the Kestrel Lock in 1887"]:
            out = await tools["cite"].acall(url=URL, quote=quote)
            print(out.raw_output.content[0].text[:90].replace("\n", " "))

asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
loaded: 21 ['navigate', 'snapshot', 'read', 'click', 'type', 'press', 'hover', 'scroll']
VERIFIED [1] <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-l
NOT VERIFIED: these words are not on <page_content untrusted="true">The Kestrel Lock</page
```

The clean text of a result is `out.raw_output.content[0].text`; `out.content` is the noisy `str()` of the whole result. Pass `url` to `cite` explicitly, since it is required. To use the tools in an agent, build a `FunctionAgent(tools=list(tools.values()), llm=...)` and run it inside the same session block. **Not run** (no model).

## AutoGen

```sh
pip install "autogen-ext[mcp]" autogen-agentchat "mcp<2"   # tested: autogen-ext 0.7.5, mcp 1.30.0
```

The `mcp<2` pin is needed: with `mcp` 2.3.0 installed, `from autogen_ext.tools.mcp import ...` failed in testing with `ImportError: cannot import name 'RequestContext' from 'mcp.shared.context'`.

```python
import asyncio
from autogen_ext.tools.mcp import McpWorkbench, StdioServerParams

URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html"
params = StdioServerParams(command="ostler", args=["serve", "--tools", "research"],
                           read_timeout_seconds=60)

async def main():
    async with McpWorkbench(params) as wb:  # one session = one Ostler process
        tools = await wb.list_tools()
        print("loaded:", len(tools), [t["name"] for t in tools[:8]])
        await wb.call_tool("read", {"url": URL})
        for quote in ["It opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta Ilves",
                      "Tomas Reyes designed the Kestrel Lock in 1887"]:
            r = await wb.call_tool("cite", {"url": URL, "quote": quote})
            print(r.to_text()[:90].replace("\n", " "))

asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
loaded: 21 ['navigate', 'snapshot', 'read', 'click', 'type', 'press', 'hover', 'scroll']
VERIFIED [1] <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-l
NOT VERIFIED: these words are not on <page_content untrusted="true">The Kestrel Lock</page
```

A `NOT VERIFIED` result comes back with `is_error = True` on the `ToolResult` rather than as an exception. `AssistantAgent` takes the workbench through its `workbench` parameter (the parameter exists; the model call was **not run**):

```python
async with McpWorkbench(params) as wb:
    agent = AssistantAgent("researcher", model_client=model_client, workbench=wb)
    await agent.run(task="Read the Kestrel Lock page and cite who designed it.")
```

## Other frameworks

Anything that speaks MCP over stdio works the same way: launch `ostler serve --tools research` (or `forms`, or `all`), keep the process for the whole task, and give the model the tools. For Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and VS Code, see [use with your agent](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/agents.html). Not tested here: CrewAI, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Semantic Kernel, and non-Python frameworks.


---

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/research-with-citations.html

# Research with checked citations

Ostler checks a quotation against the text of a page it actually read in this session, and lists the pages it could not read. An agent using `read`, `cite` and `evidence` can then answer with only the claims that were verified, and say plainly what it could not check. It runs on your machine, in your Chrome, from any MCP client such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor.

**What this does not do.** `cite` proves that the words are on the page. It does not prove that the claim is true, that the page is a good source, or that the agent quoted in context. Quote matching is not fact-checking.

## The workflow

Three tools carry it. They are in the `research` profile; `--tools research` pins them, and the default `--tools auto` reveals them after the first `read`. All 32 tools are in the [tools reference](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/tools.html#research-profile-research).

| step | tool | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `read` | Opens a page and returns the best passages for your `query`, with a fetch time and a content hash. The page text is stored for this session. |
| 2 | `cite` | Takes a `url` and a `quote` (12 or more characters). Returns `VERIFIED` with a link a person can open to check the words, or `NOT VERIFIED`, `NOT READ` or `TOO SHORT`. |
| 3 | `evidence` | Lists verified citations, pages read but not cited, and gaps: paywall, bot wall, robots.txt refusal, HTTP error, empty page. Call it before answering. |

`open_many` reads up to 10 URLs at once in a scratch tab and obeys robots.txt. `search` finds pages to read; it needs a provider (`OSTLER_SEARXNG_URL`, or `OSTLER_SEARCH_PROVIDER=brave` with `OSTLER_BRAVE_API_KEY`) and has been tested against mock servers only.

## Try it on the bundled pages

Nothing leaves your machine. Install Ostler from source ([install guide](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/install.html)), then start the local fixture server:

```sh
ostler fixtures        # serves http://127.0.0.1:8787, loopback only
```

Add `ostler serve --tools research` to your MCP client ([setup for each client](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/agents.html)), and give the agent this prompt:

> Find out who designed the Kestrel Lock and when it opened. Use `read`, then back every claim with `cite`, and finish with `evidence`. If a page could not be read, say so instead of guessing. Start at `http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/index.html`.

## Expected output

This is unedited tool output from `ostler 0.2.0` built from the `main` branch (no tagged release), captured on 2026-11-06 against `ostler fixtures` with `ostler serve --tools research`. Fetch times and the shown similarity score can differ on your run; the structure and verdicts should not.

### A page is read

```text
> read {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html", "query": "who designed the lock"}
Read: <page_content untrusted="true">The Kestrel Lock</page_content> — <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html</page_content> · page · 297 chars · fetched 2026-11-06T16:01:32Z · sha256:9f602117
1 of 1 passages for <page_content untrusted="true">who designed the lock</page_content>:
<page_content untrusted="true">
[p1 · The Kestrel Lock]
# The Kestrel Lock

The Kestrel Lock is a double-chamber canal lock on the Kestrel River. It opened in 1887 and was designed by [Marta Ilves](http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/marta-ilves.html).

A major restoration in 1962 was supervised by the engineer Tomas Reyes, who is sometimes wrongly credited with the original design.

See also: [Archive index](http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/index.html).
</page_content>
To use any of this in an answer, call cite with the page URL and an exact quote.
```

`<page_content untrusted="true">` marks text that came from the page. The agent is meant to treat it as data, not as instructions.

### A quote that is on the page

```text
> cite {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html", "quote": "opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta Ilves"}
VERIFIED [1] <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html</page_content> (read 2026-11-06T16:01:32Z, sha256:9f602117)
<page_content untrusted="true">opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta Ilves</page_content>
Check it yourself (best effort): http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html#:~:text=opened%20in%201887%20and%20was%20designed%20by%20Marta%20Ilves
```

The `#:~:text=` link opens the page with the quoted words highlighted, so a person can check the source without trusting the agent.

### A quote that is not on the page

The page says the 1962 restoration was supervised by Tomas Reyes, who "is sometimes wrongly credited with the original design". An agent that skims could easily write that Reyes designed the lock. Ostler rejects the claim:

```text
> cite {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html", "quote": "Tomas Reyes designed the Kestrel Lock in 1887"}
NOT VERIFIED: these words are not on <page_content untrusted="true">The Kestrel Lock</page_content>. Do not state this claim as sourced; quote the page's own words, not a summary.
Closest text on the page (similarity 0.48): <page_content untrusted="true">The Kestrel Lock The Kestrel Lock is a double</page_content>
```

The agent is told not to state the claim as sourced. In this run the "closest text" it offered was the page's title and the start of its first sentence, at similarity 0.48, which is not the sentence that matters. Treat that hint as a pointer to look again, not as the answer.

### A page that cannot be fully read

```text
> read {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/paywall.html"}
Read: <page_content untrusted="true">The Valley Courier: the cost of restoring the Kestrel Lock</page_content> — <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/paywall.html</page_content> · page · 293 chars · fetched 2026-11-06T16:01:32Z · sha256:8952387c
PAYWALL: only a teaser is readable here. Do not state what the rest of the article says; report it as a gap.
<page_content untrusted="true">
# The cost of restoring the Kestrel Lock

The Valley Courier (synthetic). When the council approved the Kestrel Lock restoration, nobody expected the bill to become the talk of the valley...

## Subscribe to keep reading

This article is for subscribers only. Sign in or subscribe to read the rest.
</page_content>
To use any of this in an answer, call cite with the page URL and an exact quote.
```

### What the agent may say

```text
> evidence {}
EVIDENCE: 2 page(s) read, 1 verified citation(s), 1 gap kind(s). 2 sources: 1 ok; 1 gaps: 1 paywalled

Verified (state only what these support):
[1] <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html</page_content> — <page_content untrusted="true">opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta Ilves</page_content>
    check: http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html#:~:text=opened%20in%201887%20and%20was%20designed%20by%20Marta%20Ilves

Gaps (not read; say so rather than guess what they contain):
- paywalled: http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/paywall.html

Read but not cited:
- <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/paywall.html</page_content>
```

The paywalled page is a gap: the agent must report that it could not read it, and must not guess what the article says. In this output the same page also appears under "Read but not cited"; that is how the report looks today, and it does not change the rule that a gap is not evidence.

## What it checks, and what it does not

| Checked | Not checked |
|---|---|
| The quoted words are on a page read in this session (Markdown around them is ignored, `...` marks an omission). | That the claim is true, current or well sourced. |
| The agent cannot cite a page it never read: `NOT READ` is an error. | Whether the quote is used in its original context. |
| A changed page invalidates earlier citations: `read` reports `CHANGED` and `evidence` lists them as stale. | Pages behind a bot wall or paywall: these are reported as gaps, not worked around. |
| Text aimed at the agent is flagged (`ATTENTION`), not obeyed. | PDFs: there is no PDF text layer. |

Other limits today: pages are read one at a time, sources are not kept across sessions, and `search` has not been run against a live provider in tests.

## Provenance and evidence

- Tool behaviour: [tools reference](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/tools.html#research-profile-research) and the [cookbook recipe](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/cookbook.html#13-research-with-citations-that-are-checked).
- Evidence for these tools is a transcript on bundled fixtures, plus the project's tests. There is no published accuracy evaluation of citation checking on real pages yet; see [benchmarks](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html) for what has and has not been measured.
- Source code: [github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler).

## Next step

For forms rather than research, see [verified form filling](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/forms.html).

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/cookbook.html

# Cookbook

Recipes for what you can do with Ostler **today**. Each one names the tools involved, a prompt to give your agent, the flags that make it safe, and what Ostler will and will not tell you. Back to the [README](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/README.md); tool details are in [TOOLS.md](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/TOOLS.md).

Ostler is a general browser first: the 16 core tools (navigate, read, click, type, tabs, screenshots) cover recipes 1 to 6 with no form or research tools. Two layers add verification on top: research with citations that are checked (recipe 13) and a form engine that reads every value back (recipes 7 to 11).

Everything marked **planned** at the end is built as a library but is not an MCP tool yet. It is listed so you know what not to expect.

## Contents

| # | recipe | tools |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Read a page and answer a question](#1-read-a-page-and-answer-a-question) | `navigate` `snapshot` |
| 2 | [Compare several pages side by side](#2-compare-several-pages-side-by-side) | `tabs` `snapshot` `context` |
| 3 | [Check a web app after a change (QA)](#3-check-a-web-app-after-a-change-qa) | `navigate` `click` `wait_for` `look` `screenshot` |
| 4 | [Get past a cookie wall or modal](#4-get-past-a-cookie-wall-or-modal) | `look` `click` |
| 5 | [Log in once, reuse the session](#5-log-in-once-reuse-the-session) | `--profile-dir` `wait_for_human` |
| 6 | [Handle a CAPTCHA honestly](#6-handle-a-captcha-honestly) | `wait_for_human` `--headed` |
| 7 | [Fill a form and verify it](#7-fill-a-form-and-verify-it) | `form_inspect` `form_fill` `form_submit` |
| 8 | [Fill a multi-step wizard](#8-fill-a-multi-step-wizard) | `form_fill` `form_submit` |
| 9 | [Never fill the same form twice](#9-never-fill-the-same-form-twice) | `memory_remember` `--learn` |
| 10 | [Submit only with your approval](#10-submit-only-with-your-approval) | `--require-confirm-submit` |
| 11 | [Hand a form to another agent over A2A](#11-hand-a-form-to-another-agent-over-a2a) | `ostler a2a` |
| 12 | [Keep a run cheap](#12-keep-a-run-cheap) | `--tools` `stats` `snapshot` delta |
| 13 | [Research with citations that are checked](#13-research-with-citations-that-are-checked) | `search` `open_many` `read` `cite` `evidence` |

## 1. Read a page and answer a question

**Use it for:** documentation lookups, reading an article, checking what a page says.

**Prompt:** "Open https://example.com/docs/limits and tell me the rate limit for the free plan. Quote the sentence."

`navigate` returns the page state with interactive elements. `snapshot` returns the page as text with element refs. On a long page, pass the ref of a heading to read only that section, and use `delta` on later calls to see only what changed. Page text arrives wrapped as untrusted content, so instructions inside a page are data, not commands.

**Be aware:** `snapshot` gives your agent the text; it does not check that the agent's quote is on the page. For answers that must be sourced, use `read` and `cite` ([recipe 13](#13-research-with-citations-that-are-checked)).

## 2. Compare several pages side by side

**Use it for:** comparing plans, specs or release notes from three sources.

**Prompt:** "Open these three pricing pages in separate tabs. Write down each plan's price in the shared notes, then give me a table."

`tabs` with `new <url>` opens each page; all tabs share cookies and the `context` notepad, so the agent can store `plan_a=$12/mo` and read it back after switching tabs. Keep notes short: `context` is for facts, not page dumps. Popups open as new tabs under the same policy.

## 3. Check a web app after a change (QA)

**Use it for:** a quick end-to-end check of your own app on localhost or staging.

**Prompt:** "Start at http://localhost:3000, sign in with the test account, add an item to the cart, and tell me whether the cart badge says 1. Take a screenshot at the end."

`click`, `type`, `press` and `wait_for` drive the flow. `wait_for` waits for text to appear or disappear or for a selector, so the agent asserts on what the page shows instead of sleeping. `look` and `screenshot` give a visual record. Allow only your own origin: `ostler serve --allow-domain localhost`.

**Be aware:** there is no console-error or failed-request report over MCP yet (`diagnostics` is [planned](#planned-not-yet-mcp-tools)).

## 4. Get past a cookie wall or modal

**Prompt:** "Dismiss anything blocking the page, then continue."

`look` returns a screenshot with every clickable element boxed and numbered, plus a legend (`e6 button "Accept" → ...`). Elements hidden under a modal or banner are left out and counted, so the agent knows to close the overlay first rather than click something it cannot reach.

## 5. Log in once, reuse the session

**Use it for:** sites that need a login for every task.

```sh
ostler serve --headed --profile-dir ~/.ostler/profile
```

Log in yourself in the visible window (including any 2FA). Later runs with the same `--profile-dir` start already signed in. Ostler does not store your password and never types a credential you did not supply.

## 6. Handle a CAPTCHA honestly

When a CAPTCHA or verification wall blocks the page, Ostler reports it (a `CHALLENGE:` line) and does not try to solve or disguise itself ([ADR-0009](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-challenges-are-handed-off.md)). With `--headed`, `wait_for_human` pauses until you complete it in the browser window, then the agent continues. Over A2A the task moves to `input-required`.

## 7. Fill a form and verify it

**Prompt:** "Open http://127.0.0.1:8787/dependent.html (from `ostler fixtures`) and fill the shipping form for Ada Lovelace in Germany, Bavaria."

```text
> form_inspect                      typed fields: kind, label, required, options, errors
> form_fill {"Country": "Germany", "State": "Bavaria", "Recipient": "Ada Lovelace"}
Filled 3/3 fields (form e2).
  OK e4 "Country" = "de"
  OK e5 "State / region" = "by"     <- options loaded after Country changed
> form_submit                       Submitted | Advanced | NOT ACCEPTED + the page's messages
```

Every value is read back from the live page. A key that matches nothing is `UNMATCHED`, a tie is `ambiguous`, and a rejected submit returns the page's own words. Treat `UNMATCHED` and `NOT ACCEPTED` as the signal to stop and ask, not to retry blindly.

## 8. Fill a multi-step wizard

Call `form_fill` then `form_submit` per step. A result of `Advanced` means the page moved to the next step; run `form_inspect` again to get its fields. Conditional sections that appear after an answer are picked up by the next inspect.

## 9. Never fill the same form twice

```sh
ostler serve --learn
```

Save facts once (`memory_remember email ada@example.com`) or let `--learn` save non-sensitive values after an accepted submit. Memory defaults to `--memory auto` (Qdrant if reachable, else a local file). With `auto`, `form_fill` fills the remaining required fields from memory, and `form_inspect` tells the agent what worked on this site before. Memory lives in Qdrant or an encrypted local file, is scoped per `--tenant`, and secrets are refused. See [MEMORY.md](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/MEMORY.md).

## 10. Submit only with your approval

```sh
ostler serve --require-confirm-submit
```

The agent can fill and verify, but `form_submit` is held until you confirm. Use it for anything with consequences: applications, orders, messages. Pair it with `--allow-domain` so the agent can only reach the sites you name.

## 11. Hand a form to another agent over A2A

```sh
ostler a2a --allow-domain example.com
```

Another agent sends a task over A2A v1.0 and gets `input-required` back when a field is missing or a submit needs confirmation. See [A2A.md](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/a2a.html).

## 12. Keep a run cheap

- `--tools auto` (default) shows 16 core tools (about 5.3 KB), reveals `cite`, `evidence`, `search`, `open_many`, `extract` and `links` after the first `read`, and the form and memory tools once a page has fields. `--tools core` keeps the schema smallest; `--tools research` pins the research set.
- `read` with a `query` returns only the best-matching passages, so a long page costs a few hundred tokens instead of the whole page.
- Use `snapshot` with `delta` and heading refs rather than re-reading whole pages.
- Call `stats` to see calls, time and estimated tokens for the session.
- Form recipes beat per-field clicking: 3 calls versus 22 on the 20-field fixture, measured on a scripted agent ([BENCHMARKS.md](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html)).

## 13. Research with citations that are checked

**Use it for:** any question whose answer will be relied on: a fact, a comparison, a "what does the source say".

**Prompt:** "Find out who designed the Kestrel Lock and when it opened. Use `read`, then back every claim with `cite`, and finish with `evidence`. If a page could not be read, say so instead of guessing." (Try it on the bundled pages: `ostler fixtures`, then start at `http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/index.html`.)

```text
> read {"url": ".../kestrel-lock.html", "query": "who designed the lock"}
Read: "The Kestrel Lock" — .../kestrel-lock.html · page · 297 chars · fetched 2026-11-06T14:44:22Z · sha256:9f602117
[p1 · The Kestrel Lock] ... It opened in 1887 and was designed by [Marta Ilves](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/.../marta-ilves.html). ...

> cite {"url": ".../kestrel-lock.html", "quote": "opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta Ilves"}
VERIFIED [1] .../kestrel-lock.html (read 2026-11-06T14:44:22Z, sha256:9f602117)
Check it yourself (best effort): .../kestrel-lock.html#:~:text=opened%20in%201887%20and%20was%20designed%20by%20Marta%20Ilves

> cite {"url": ".../kestrel-lock.html", "quote": "Tomas Reyes designed the Kestrel Lock in 1887"}
NOT VERIFIED: these words are not on "The Kestrel Lock". Do not state this claim as sourced ...
```

What this gives you that a page-to-markdown API does not:

- **Nothing can be cited that was not read.** `cite` checks the quote against the stored text of a page read in this session. `NOT READ` and `NOT VERIFIED` are errors, and the second shows the closest text on the page.
- **Gaps are reported, not hidden.** A paywalled page (teaser only), a verification wall, a robots.txt refusal, an HTTP error or an empty page is recorded. `evidence` lists them next to the verified citations, so "I could not read X" is part of the answer.
- **Changed pages invalidate their citations.** Read the same URL again and, if the text differs, `read` says `CHANGED` and `evidence` lists the earlier citations as stale.
- **Text aimed at your agent is flagged**, not obeyed: the header says `ATTENTION`, and a citation inside such text carries a warning.
- **It runs on your machine and your browser.** With `--profile-dir`, pages behind your login are readable; Ostler sends nothing to a third party, though your MCP client may pass what a tool returns to its model provider.

`open_many` reads up to 10 URLs at once in a scratch tab (your tab is untouched), obeying robots.txt and per-host spacing, and returns the best passages from each. `search` needs a provider: set `OSTLER_SEARXNG_URL` (a SearXNG instance) or `OSTLER_SEARCH_PROVIDER=brave` with `OSTLER_BRAVE_API_KEY`, then restart the server. `extract` returns tables as rows and lists with a `PARTIAL: 5 of 13` verdict when the page says there is more.

**Be aware:** `cite` proves the words are on the page, not that the claim is true. Pages are read one at a time, there is no PDF text layer, and sources are not kept across sessions. A search provider has been tested against mock servers only.

## Planned, not yet MCP tools

These exist as libraries in the workspace (`ostler-workflow`, the memory `source` kind, the diagnostics collector) and are covered by tests and a fixture pack, but **no MCP tool exposes them yet**. Do not write prompts that depend on them.

| recipe | needs | status |
|---|---|---|
| Assert a postcondition after a click ("the page now shows step 2") | `expect` | library only |
| See console errors and failed requests | `diagnostics` | per-tab capture built, no tool |
| Remember what you read across sessions | source memory | library only |

Tracking: [BUILD-PLAN.md](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/BUILD-PLAN.md).


---

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/forms.html

# Forms and verification

Ostler's form engine is built so the model states intent once and the engine does the mechanics: it resolves each key to a field, fills in order, lets dependent controls appear, reads every value back, and reports what actually happened.

## The three-call flow

1. **`form_inspect`** returns typed fields: kind, label, required, options, pattern, current value, and any error. It also lists submit controls and says what memory knows about this form.
2. **`form_fill`** takes `{label | name | ref: value}` for the whole form.
3. **`form_submit`** clicks the submit or next control and reports the outcome.

Dependent dropdowns, multi-step wizards, input masks, comboboxes, shadow DOM and same-origin iframes are handled inside these calls. See the [tools reference](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/tools.html#forms-profile-forms) for parameters.

## How a key becomes a field

Keys are resolved in this order: exact ref, then name or id, then label, then fuzzy label. A key can match by ref, name, label or fuzzy label, and keys are resolved against every visible field once, so an ambiguous key cannot win by elimination.

- **Ambiguity is reported, never guessed.** If two fields match equally well, the report says `ambiguous` and asks for the ref. `email` finds "E-mail address", because a key equal to a run of the label's words written together matches, but two equally plausible fields are still refused.
- **A key that matches nothing is `UNMATCHED`.** It is not dropped silently, and the fill report only counts as OK if no key was unmatched.
- **Forms re-mounted by a framework are followed.**

## How a value is normalised

The engine converts the value for the field before writing it:

| you send | field | written |
|---|---|---|
| `"Germany"` | select | the option index for that option text |
| `"March 5, 2001"` | date | `2001-03-05` |
| `"3:30 PM"` | time | `15:30` |
| `03/04/2024` | date | **refused as ambiguous** (day-first or month-first), so the agent must say which |

Fields are filled in document order and the form is **re-inspected after every field**, so a dependent control (State after Country) appears before it is needed.

## Verification: read it back

After writing a field, the engine reads the value back from the live page and compares it by field type.

- A value the page rewrote or cleared fails. A `datetime-local` must read back as the requested instant.
- A combobox must show the option you asked for. A longer option that merely contains it is a mismatch ("United States" versus "United States Minor Outlying Islands"), and the in-page picker only picks an exact, normalised option label, listing the options otherwise.
- Values the page legitimately reformats, such as `(555) 123-4567`, are reported as **reformatted**, not as errors. Only exact matches and genuine reformatting pass.
- `form_fill` reports `unsettled` (a count) when the page was still busy at the end of the fill, so the verdicts can be treated with care.

Typed input is tried first, because it fires the same events a user would. If the page rejects it (masked or framework-controlled inputs), the engine retries with the native value setter plus events. Fills also send one harmless `keyup`, because some date pickers learn the text only from that event.

### Verified, then submitted empty

Just before clicking submit, `form_submit` re-reads the fields it verified and reports any the page cleared or rewrote in between as `CHANGED BEFORE SUBMIT`. This was added after a date picker was reported verified and then submitted empty.

## Submit results

| result | meaning |
|---|---|
| `Submitted` | the page accepted it: a new URL, or new confirmation text appeared after the click (for example a form that posts in the background and says "Thanks!" in place) |
| `Advanced` | the page moved to the next step of a wizard; repeat inspect, fill, submit |
| `NOT ACCEPTED` | the page reported problems, and the page's own messages follow |
| `SERVER ERROR` | the site answered the submit with an HTTP error (4xx/5xx) and showed no validation messages. The data may or may not have been stored: do not report it as submitted and do not retry blindly; check with `snapshot` or ask the user |
| `Nothing changed` | the form stayed put and said nothing visible. Check with `snapshot`; do not resubmit blindly, because it may have gone through |

With several forms on a page, `form_submit` with no `form` or `control` submits the form `form_fill` last filled; if none was filled it refuses and lists the forms rather than guessing the first.

A thank-you page that still has an optional input (a newsletter box, a search) counts as `Submitted`, not `Advanced`, unless something on it is required, it has a step counter, or it has a "next" button.

## Errors you can only see

Fields marked invalid only by colour (a red border, outline or glow, or red message text with no ARIA or class) and floating toasts or banners are reported as field and page errors. An error that was already on a field before the fill is flagged as possibly stale. An error message belongs to the field it follows, not to every field sharing a wrapper, and Bootstrap 3 `.help-block` is help text unless the group is `.has-error`.

## Pages without a `<form>`

Only real action buttons are submit candidates. The header's "Search" button, anything inside `header`, `nav` or `role=search`, and type-less buttons whose label says nothing about submitting ("Show tips") do not count.

## Dates and pickers

Calendar date pickers on read-only inputs are handled heuristically: when a text field is read-only and the value is a date, the engine opens the popup, navigates months and clicks the day. It fails with a reason, not silently, when no popup or navigation is found. The heuristic looks for a month header, previous and next controls and day cells. Dropdown-only and year-only pickers are not handled.

## Seeing the page

Two tools help when a form is not obvious:

- **`look`** returns a screenshot with every clickable element boxed and numbered, and a legend such as `e6 button "Send" -> submits the form`.
- **`snapshot`** with a heading's ref reads just that section.

A CAPTCHA, hCaptcha, Turnstile or "verify you are human" wall is reported with a `CHALLENGE:` line at the top of the result. The agent should stop retrying and ask you; with `--headed`, `wait_for_human` waits while you complete it. Ostler never solves or bypasses these ([ADR-0009](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-challenges-are-handed-off.md)).

## What it does not handle

- Cross-origin iframes and closed shadow roots are invisible to the injected runtime.
- 2FA, CAPTCHA solving and anti-bot evasion are out of scope.
- Fill on very large forms (thousands of fields) is slow, because every key re-reads the form.
- It has been evaluated on local fixtures, not on the open web. See [Benchmarks](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html).

## When not to use Ostler

Ostler is a form-filling browser for an agent working on your behalf, on one machine. It is the wrong tool when:

- **The site walls off automation.** CAPTCHA, Cloudflare/Turnstile, "verify you are human" pages and search-engine bot checks are reported with a `CHALLENGE:` line and handed to a person. Ostler never solves or bypasses them, and it is not built to avoid detection: there is no stealth patching, fingerprint spoofing, residential proxy or IP rotation. A site that blocks headless or datacenter Chrome will block Ostler. `--headed` plus a persistent `--profile-dir` lets *you* pass a check once; it does not make a bot wall go away.
- **You need scale.** Each server drives one local Chrome (tabs share its cookies and profile). It is not a remote or cloud browser farm, not a crawler, and not meant for bulk scraping or high-volume account creation. More sessions means more servers, each with its own profile and its own memory use (see [Benchmarks](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html)).
- **The flow needs an identity Ostler does not have.** There is no mailbox, phone number, SMS/OTP receiver or authenticator: one-time codes, email-link verification, passkeys, hardware keys and 2FA prompts need a person. Passwords and card numbers are never read back or remembered; sensitive fields are refused and the agent is told to ask you. It does not create accounts on your behalf out of thin air.
- **The page is outside what the injected runtime can see.** Cross-origin iframes (many hosted card fields), closed shadow roots, canvas-drawn UIs, native OS dialogs and file pickers, and desktop apps are not reachable. A control that stays disabled until a person scrolls or hovers is reported as disabled rather than worked around.
- **A wrong submit is expensive and nobody is checking.** Ostler verifies every value by reading it back and refuses to call a submit a success without evidence, but it cannot know whether a form means what it says. For payments, legal acceptance and anything irreversible, run with `--require-confirm-submit` and review the result yourself.

When Ostler cannot finish, it says which field and why (rejected value with the page's own message, hidden or disabled control, key not found) and points at `screenshot` for the element; it does not report a partial fill as done.

## Design records

The reasoning, with the alternatives that were rejected, is in [ADR-0004](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/adr/0004-injected-runtime.md) (injected runtime) and [ADR-0005](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/docs/adr/0005-form-ir-and-verification.md) (form model and verification). A summary is on the [Architecture](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/architecture.html) page.


---

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/memory.html

# Memory and privacy

Memory is optional. Browsing and form filling need no account and no key. When you turn it on, Ostler saves facts you told it, which fact fills which field on which site, and what went wrong on a form, in your own [Qdrant](https://qdrant.tech).

This page is exact about what is stored, what is encrypted, and what is **not** hidden. The sealing, local-embedding and per-tenant-token features below are described in the changelog's *Unreleased* section: they are on `main` and not in a tagged release yet. **Unreleased: main branch, not a tagged release.**

## What is stored

Three Qdrant collections, multi-tenant through a `tenant` payload index:

| collection | holds | never holds |
|---|---|---|
| `ostler_profile` | facts you saved (`email`, `company`, …) | passwords, card numbers, anything that looks sensitive |
| `ostler_playbooks` | per site and form: which fact fills which field, with wins, losses and last verified time | the values themselves |
| `ostler_episodes` | what went wrong on a form, so it is not repeated | secrets |

Ostler sends no telemetry. Disk holds nothing by default, apart from a Chrome profile if you pass `--profile-dir`, and the config and key files described below.

Secrets are refused by the memory API (password, token and card-like keys, and card-number-like values), sensitive fields are never auto-filled from memory nor stored by `--learn`, and sensitive values are masked in tool output. Detection is heuristic (names, `autocomplete` tokens, digit patterns): a secret stored under an innocuous key with an innocuous value will not be caught. Learned values never overwrite facts you saved.

`--learn` is off by default. Ostler records *how* forms were filled automatically (structure only), but stores *your data* only when you opt in with `--learn` or call `memory_remember`.

## Where your data goes

Five places data can travel. Only the last two involve Qdrant, and only if you turn memory on.

| step | where it goes | what crosses | what you control |
|---|---|---|---|
| Browsing | Chrome on your machine talks directly to the sites you visit. | The page requests Chrome makes. Ostler sends no telemetry. | `--allow-domain` limits every request the browser makes; `--profile-dir` decides whether logins persist. |
| Tool output to your agent | Over stdio to the MCP client that launched Ostler (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code). | Page text, the values read back from form fields, and verification reports. Sensitive values are masked in tool output, but detection is heuristic. | Your client decides what happens next. **A client normally forwards tool output to its model provider**, so treat anything a tool returns as visible to that provider and check the client's own privacy settings. |
| Search | The SearXNG instance or Brave API you configure for `search`. | The search query. | Without a provider configured, `search` sends nothing. |
| Embeddings | By default, Qdrant Cloud Inference. With `--embeddings ollama`, your own machine. **Unreleased: main branch, not a tagged release.** | With cloud inference, the field text to be embedded. | `--embeddings ollama` keeps text local. |
| Stored memory | Your Qdrant. | Facts you saved, playbooks and episodes. Sealed on your machine before upload by default. **Unreleased: main branch, not a tagged release.** | `--seal`, `--embeddings`, `--isolation`; `memory_forget` deletes. |

Secrets are the part to be careful about. Memory refuses password-, token- and card-like keys and card-number-like values, but that check is a heuristic: a secret saved under an innocuous key and value would not be caught, and it would then also be part of what a later tool call returns to your agent.

## Sealing: encrypt before it reaches Qdrant

With memory in Qdrant, payloads are **sealed on your machine by default** (`--seal auto`). **Unreleased: main branch, not a tagged release.**

- Fact values, descriptions, playbooks and episodes are encrypted with **AES-256-GCM**, with the point id bound in as associated data.
- Site names, field labels, profile keys and fingerprints are replaced by **keyed hashes (HMAC-SHA-256)**, and point ids are keyed too, so filters still work but the server cannot test guesses ("passport number") against what it stores.
- Episodes are **redacted before** they are embedded or stored: emails, runs of four or more digits (phones, PIN codes, card numbers) and URL query strings are masked, in addition to the values the agent typed.
- The key lives in `OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY` or an owner-only `memory.key` next to the config file, created atomically on the first start. That start only creates a key after Qdrant was reached and holds no sealed memory for your tenant; with Qdrant down it refuses (start Qdrant, restore a backup with `ostler memory key import`, or pass `--allow-new-key` for a genuine first-time setup). **Back it up: there is no recovery.** If you lose it, sealed memory is unreadable.
- `--seal on` forces it; `--seal off` opts out (and `ostler doctor` and `serve` warn that anyone who can read your Qdrant can then read your saved facts and the sites you use).

### What is hidden, and what is not

| | someone who can read your Qdrant (operator, leaked key, backup) sees |
|---|---|
| Fact values and descriptions | encrypted |
| Playbooks and episodes (contents) | encrypted; episodes are also redacted of emails and numbers |
| Site names, field labels, profile keys, fingerprints | keyed hashes only |
| **The vector** | **visible.** With `--embeddings cloud`, the field text is sent to Qdrant Cloud Inference to be embedded, and vectors of labels reveal roughly what they say. Use `--embeddings ollama` to keep text local |
| **Tenant name** | visible |
| **Win and loss counters, timing, point counts** | visible |

The key is, in order of precedence, the `OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY` variable, or the store chosen by `key_store` (`OSTLER_KEY_STORE`): `file` (default, owner-only `memory.key`) or `keychain` (macOS Keychain / Linux Secret Service). **Unreleased: main branch, not a tagged release.** `ostler memory key export --yes-print` and `ostler memory key import` back it up and restore it.

### Memory written before sealing

Memory saved before sealing was on is invisible until you run:

```sh
ostler config set seal on
ostler memory seal
```

Saved facts are copied into sealed form and read back to check them before the old plaintext points are deleted, so it is safe to interrupt and run again. **Learned skills and episodes from that time are dropped** and relearned.

## Local embeddings

By default Ostler embeds text with Qdrant Cloud Inference (`sentence-transformers/all-minilm-l6-v2`, 384 dimensions). To keep the text on your machine, embed locally with Ollama: **Unreleased: main branch, not a tagged release.**

```sh
ostler serve --embeddings ollama --embedding-model <model> --embedding-dim <dims>
```

| `--embeddings` | where text is embedded | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `cloud` (default) | inside Qdrant Cloud Inference | needs Inference enabled on the cluster. Field text is sent to Qdrant. Covered by request-shape tests; **not run against a live Cloud cluster** by the maintainers |
