Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html

# Benchmarks

Everything below was measured by `ostler-bench` on one machine and is reproducible with the commands at the end. The harness prints its own assumptions with every table. If a number here disagrees with what you measure, trust yours and open an issue.

**Machine:** Apple M2, 8 cores, 8 GB RAM, macOS 26.6, Chrome 156, Qdrant (latest release binary at the time), single machine, everything over localhost.
**Date:** 2026-10-30 (section 5: 2026-11-02). **Revision:** not recorded. The raw files in `bench-results/` record the version string `ostler 0.2.0` and the date, not a commit, and `git log` shows the history of this document, not the revision that was measured. Re-runs should note `git rev-parse HEAD`.

## What these benchmarks do and do not show

- They run against the **local fixtures** in `crates/ostler-fixtures/fixtures/` (the form benchmark drives 10 of the 49 form fixture pages, built to reproduce documented form-filling failure modes: basic, validation, dependent, wizard, controlled, combobox, shadow, iframe, longform, types). They show the engine handles those failure modes and what it costs. They do **not** show success rates on the open web. Section 7 checks seven live practice pages (correctness of what the tool claims, no model, small corpus); a real-model evaluation on a wider set of real sites is the next milestone ([roadmap](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/#limits)).
- The "per-field" baseline is **our own engine driven the way snapshot-per-action tools are driven** (one call per field, each returning a full page snapshot). It isolates the effect of the interaction pattern. It is **not** a measurement of Playwright MCP, agent-browser or any other product (section 5 runs Playwright MCP and Chrome DevTools MCP for real). Tools that offer batched form fills would sit between the two columns.
- LLM prices, LLM turn latency and cloud prices are **illustrative parameters** (flags on the harness). Token counts are `bytes / 4`, an estimate.

## 1. Forms: tool calls, tokens, cost, latency

Median of 3 runs. `calls` = agent tool calls. `in tok` = total input tokens the model reads across all turns (every turn re-reads the conversation). `$ cached` = LLM cost with prompt caching (cache reads at 0.1x, writes at 1.25x) at the illustrative $3 / $15 per Mtok. `e2e` = tool time + turns x 3 s.

**Baseline and mode:** `engine` is Ostler's form engine. `per-field` is the same engine driven one call per field, not another product. Scripted, no LLM in the loop, local fixtures, one machine.

| scenario | mode | calls | out tok | in tok | tool ms | e2e s | $ cached |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| basic contact form | engine | 3 | 201 | 11,300 | 473 | 12.5 | 0.0169 |
| basic contact form | per-field | 6 | 695 | 21,866 | 499 | 21.5 | 0.0236 |
| validation (3 rules) | engine | 3 | 177 | 11,218 | 491 | 12.5 | 0.0166 |
| validation (3 rules) | per-field | 5 | 498 | 18,021 | 490 | 18.5 | 0.0211 |
| dependent dropdowns | engine | 3 | 229 | 11,400 | 845 | 12.8 | 0.0170 |
| dependent dropdowns | per-field | 6 | 879 | 22,679 | 852 | 21.9 | 0.0245 |
| 3-step wizard | engine | 7 | 385 | 23,917 | 1,014 | 25.0 | 0.0238 |
| 3-step wizard | per-field | 9 | 987 | 33,244 | 1,022 | 31.0 | 0.0302 |
| controlled inputs | engine | 3 | 164 | 11,199 | 472 | 12.5 | 0.0166 |
| controlled inputs | per-field | 5 | 457 | 17,884 | 488 | 18.5 | 0.0210 |
| custom combobox | engine | 3 | 128 | 11,079 | 423 | 12.4 | 0.0162 |
| custom combobox | per-field | 3 | 184 | 11,193 | 421 | 12.4 | 0.0165 |
| shadow DOM | engine | 3 | 158 | 11,160 | 467 | 12.5 | 0.0165 |
| shadow DOM | per-field | 4 | 331 | 14,470 | 469 | 15.5 | 0.0188 |
| same-origin iframe | engine | 3 | 169 | 11,172 | 450 | 12.4 | 0.0165 |
| same-origin iframe | per-field | 4 | 377 | 14,586 | 461 | 15.5 | 0.0190 |
| **long form (20 fields)** | **engine** | **3** | **585** | **12,544** | **1,055** | **13.1** | **0.0210** |
| **long form (20 fields)** | **per-field** | **22** | **8,337** | **166,358** | **1,113** | **70.1** | **0.1050** |
| rich inputs (9 fields) | engine | 3 | 339 | 11,732 | 658 | 12.7 | 0.0179 |

All 19 rows completed successfully (the server received the expected submission). The per-field baseline cannot drive the `rich inputs` page (radio and checkbox groups have no single control to address), so it is omitted there.

**Totals over the 9 scenarios both modes support:** engine 31 calls / 117k tokens / $0.161; per-field 64 calls / 324k tokens / $0.280. Ratio per-field/engine: **2.1x calls, 2.8x tokens, 1.8x latency, 1.7x cost.**

### What this says, honestly

1. **The advantage scales with form size.** Small forms (2-4 fields): ~1.3-2x. A 20-field form: **7.3x fewer calls, 13x fewer input tokens, 5.0x cheaper, 5.4x faster end to end.** Per-field cost grows with fields x conversation length (quadratic-ish); the engine path stays at 3 calls.
2. **End-to-end time is dominated by LLM turns, not the browser.** Tool time is 0.4-1.1 s of a 12-25 s task. Making the browser faster barely moves the total; **removing round-trips does.** This is why the design optimises call count and output size before raw browser speed.
3. **A fixed floor exists.** Tool schemas (~1,138 tokens at the `all` profile when this was measured; the 21-tool set is now about 5.9 KB, roughly 1.5k tokens, see the README) plus the base prompt are re-read on every turn. That is why 3-field forms look similar across modes; `--tools core|forms` shrinks it.

## 2. Browser footprint and startup

One real task (navigate + fill + submit on the 20-field form), median of 3. Memory is **physical footprint** on macOS (`footprint`), PSS on Linux. Summed RSS would read ~3.3x higher on macOS because shared pages are counted per process, so it is not used.

| profile | start ms | processes | memory MiB | task ms | success |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| default | 631 | 10 | 658 | 585 | 100% |
| lean (`--lean`) | 565 | 10 | 412 | 587 | 100% |

`--lean` (lean Chrome flags + no image/font/media downloads) cuts memory by 37% with no change in task time. Site isolation stays on. Screenshots omit images in this mode.

A latency bug found by these benchmarks and fixed: the page runtime's own settle-polling reset its own quiet-timer, so every action waited the 3 s cap. After the fix, `about:blank` round-trips went from 3,031 ms to 160 ms and the e2e suite from 40 s to 7 s.

## 3. Concurrency and cost to serve

Each session is its own Chrome + MCP app. Task mix: 6 form scenarios (navigate + fill + submit), the dependent-dropdown API adds 250 ms of simulated latency. 6 tasks per session.

| sessions | tasks/min | p50 ms | p95 ms | mem/session MiB | CPU-s/task | compute $/1k tasks* | success |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 79 | 507 | 891 | 549 | 0.52 | 0.0064 | 100% |
| 2 | 150 | 486 | 861 | 508 | 0.48 | 0.0059 | 100% |
| 4 | 262 | 495 | 894 | 505 | 0.48 | 0.0060 | 100% |
| 8 | 354 | 605 | 960 | 483 | 0.50 | 0.0065 | 100% |
| 8 (lean) | 393 | 527 | 918 | 454 | 0.48 | 0.0061 | 100% |

\* Compute only: CPU-seconds and RAM-time at illustrative cloud prices ($0.04/vCPU-h, $0.005/GiB-h). Excludes LLM tokens, Qdrant, bandwidth, proxies, idle capacity. CPU includes Chrome startup amortised over 6 tasks.

Reading: throughput scales near-linearly to 8 sessions on 8 cores with flat latency and no failures. **Compute is ~$0.006 per 1,000 tasks; the LLM bill for the same tasks is ~$17-24 per 1,000 (section 1). Compute is roughly 0.03% of the cost of a task.**

## 4. Memory (Qdrant) at scale

Real Qdrant server, multi-tenant (`tenant` keyword payload index with `is_tenant`), 20 facts per tenant, 256-dim client-side vectors, no sealing (the harness does not wrap the store in `SealedStore`) (a 384-dim model is ~1.5x the vector bytes). Sequential queries, localhost HTTP. `sem` = `Memory::suggest` semantic path (2 requests). `key` = exact fact lookup (1 filtered scroll, no vector math).

| tenants x facts | points | load s | sem p50 | sem p95 | sem p99 | key p50 | key p95 | QPS (16 clients) | Qdrant RSS MiB |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,000 x 20 | 20,000 | 0.6 | 0.4 ms | 0.4 ms | 0.5 ms | 0.2 ms | 0.2 ms | 2,898 | 293 |
| 10,000 x 20 | 200,000 | 8.9 | 0.4 ms | 0.4 ms | 0.5 ms | 0.2 ms | 0.3 ms | 2,792 | 1,634 |
| 10,000 x 20, on-disk vectors | 200,000 | 8.4 | 0.4 ms | 0.7 ms | 0.8 ms | 0.2 ms | 0.5 ms | 2,432 | 1,298 |

- **Latency is flat from 20k to 200k points**: filtered retrieval cost follows the tenant's own 20 points, not the collection size. That is the point of the tenant index.
- **Memory is the thing to watch.** Qdrant's RSS after load-and-query was ~8 KB per point untuned at 200k (about 6.5 KB with on-disk vectors). That is a loaded-and-queried figure that includes write-path allocations, not an isolated steady-state number. Do not extrapolate it to millions of users; measure on your own restarted node. Levers: on-disk vectors (`--qdrant-on-disk`), quantization, fewer vectors per user (exact-key and `autocomplete` lookups use payload filters and need no vector).
- Over a real network add the round-trip to the cluster; Cloud Inference adds model time on embedding calls. **Neither is measured here.**

## 5. Ostler vs Playwright MCP vs Chrome DevTools MCP (same fixtures, scripted agent)

Section 1 compares Ostler with a *pattern*. This section runs the **real competitor servers** on the same local fixture pages and checks the result on the fixture server, not in the tool's reply.

**What was run (2026-11-02, Apple M2, macOS 26.6 / Darwin 25.6.0, one machine, localhost, all headless against the same Google Chrome 156.0.8078.74):**

| server | version | tools | tool definitions (est. tokens, sent every turn) |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Ostler | 0.2.0 (measured with 21 tools; the forms profile now lists 20) | 21 | 1,513 |
| Playwright MCP | npm `@playwright/mcp` 0.0.84 (reports Playwright 1.65.0-alpha-2026-10-30), `--headless --isolated --browser chrome` | 25 | 5,265 |
| Chrome DevTools MCP | npm `chrome-devtools-mcp` 1.12.0, `--headless --isolated --executablePath <Chrome>` | 32 | 7,416 |

Node v26.10.0. Median of 3 runs per task in one session per server (browser pre-launched by a warm-up call; cold start is reported separately in the JSON). Raw data: [`bench-results/compare.json`](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/bench-results/compare.json), table: [`bench-results/compare.md`](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/bench-results/compare.md).

**Method.** There is no LLM. A deterministic script plays an "ideal agent" per server: the shortest sensible sequence, with element refs parsed from the server's own output, never guessed. Each task is judged only by what the fixture server received (`GET /__submissions`): exactly one submission, equal field for field to the expected record. `steps` = tool calls. `out tokens` = bytes of tool output text / 4 (an estimate, as elsewhere in this file; no images were returned). `wall ms` = sum of tool-call times (no LLM time, no post-submit wait).

Sequences (the best idiomatic one found for each, using each server's batch fill tool):

- **Ostler:** `navigate` (observe `interactive`, which lists the controls) -> `form_fill` (label -> value map) -> `form_submit`; repeated per step on the wizard. Variant **+form_inspect**: `navigate` (observe `none`) -> `form_inspect` -> `form_fill` -> `form_submit`.
- **Playwright MCP:** `browser_navigate` -> `browser_snapshot` (in this version navigate returns the snapshot as a file link, so an MCP-only agent calls `browser_snapshot`) -> `browser_fill_form` -> `browser_click` on the submit button. Wizard: snapshot + fill + click per step. Dependent dropdowns: two `browser_fill_form` calls (country, then state and city); Playwright's select waits for the options by itself.
- **Chrome DevTools MCP:** `navigate_page` -> `take_snapshot` -> `fill_form` (`includeSnapshot=false`) -> `click`. Wizard: snapshot + fill + click per step. Dependent dropdowns: fill country, `wait_for` the text "Bavaria", fill state and city, click (a single batch failed because the option list loads after a fetch).

| task | server | steps | out tokens | wall ms | correct |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| basic form | **Ostler** | **3** | 227 | **526** | 3/3 |
| basic form | Playwright MCP | 4 | 355 | 710 | 3/3 |
| basic form | Chrome DevTools MCP | 4 | **168** | 840 | 3/3 |
| validation (3 rules) | **Ostler** | **3** | 202 | **497** | 3/3 |
| validation (3 rules) | Playwright MCP | 4 | 300 | 1,116 | 3/3 |
| validation (3 rules) | Chrome DevTools MCP | 4 | **156** | 1,287 | 3/3 |
| dependent dropdowns | **Ostler** | **3** | **238** | **844** | 3/3 |
| dependent dropdowns | Playwright MCP | 5 | 389 | 1,921 | 3/3 |
| dependent dropdowns | Chrome DevTools MCP | 6 | 476 | 1,390 | 3/3 |
| 3-step wizard | **Ostler** | **7** | 396 | **1,036** | 3/3 |
| 3-step wizard | Playwright MCP | 10 | 784 | 2,740 | 3/3 |
| 3-step wizard | Chrome DevTools MCP | 10 | **372** | 2,008 | 3/3 |
| long form (20 fields) | **Ostler** | **3** | **487** | **1,174** | 3/3 |
| long form (20 fields) | Playwright MCP | 4 | 1,132 | 2,268 | 3/3 |
| long form (20 fields) | Chrome DevTools MCP | 4 | 694 | 2,394 | 3/3 |

Totals over the 5 tasks: **Ostler 19 steps / 1,550 tokens / 4.1 s; Playwright MCP 27 / 2,960 / 8.8 s; Chrome DevTools MCP 28 / 1,866 / 7.9 s.** All three completed all 5 tasks correctly in every run. The +form_inspect variant: 24 steps, 1,496 tokens (one more call per task for about the same bytes).

### Where Ostler loses or does not differ

- **On small forms Chrome DevTools MCP returns fewer tokens** than Ostler (basic 168 vs 227, validation 156 vs 202) and about the same on the wizard (372 vs 396). Ostler's replies carry more (field read-back and verification text), which this byte count charges as cost. Whether that read-back is worth it (it is what lets an agent detect a silent failure) is **not measured here**; every tool succeeded on every run, so these fixtures never exercised it.
- **All three finish every task.** With a batch fill tool (both competitors have one) the gap is steps (about 1.4x fewer) and bytes on the largest form, not correctness. The large gaps in section 1 are against a one-field-per-call pattern, which neither competitor requires.
- **Wall time is not a browser-speed win.** Tool time here includes each server's own settling; differences of a few hundred ms are well under one LLM turn (3 s assumed in section 1). Do not read the wall column as end-to-end latency.
- **Tool definitions are the larger per-turn cost.** Ostler's 21 tool definitions are about 1.5k estimated tokens versus 5.3k and 7.4k; on a 4-call task that is repeated every turn and can exceed all of the tool output. It is a property of the tool lists, not of form handling.

### Caveats

- **No LLM.** A real model may take more or fewer steps than the scripted ideal (wrong ref, retries, extra snapshots). The script gives every server its best case; real agents on primitive tools usually do worse, which this does not show.
- **Fixtures only, 5 tasks, one machine, one Chrome, headless.** None of the 49 form fixture pages' hostile behaviours (CAPTCHA, shadow DOM, comboboxes, rich inputs) are run here; the competitors may or may not handle those, and that is **not measured**. No real sites.
- **Token counts are bytes / 4**, not a tokenizer. Playwright snapshots and Ostler observations differ in format, so the ratio is approximate.
- **Versions move.** Playwright MCP changes its snapshot-on-navigate behaviour between releases (this version links a file); re-run with `PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_VERSION=latest`. The sequences are my best attempt per server, not blessed by their authors. If you find a shorter one, open an issue.
- Cold start (server + Chrome launch) is in the JSON but not tabled: it varied 0.7-7.7 s between runs, mostly Node start-up and package loading, and is too noisy to rank.

## 6. Realistic-forms suite (correctness, not cost)

`ostler-bench suite` runs 30 form tasks through `form_inspect` / `form_fill` / `form_submit` (the MCP tool layer) against local fixtures that copy how real sites structure these forms: multi-step checkout with a billing-same-as toggle, an ATS application with resume upload and EEO selects, tax-portal style split date-of-birth selects with PAN/Aadhaar masks and state-to-district dependent selects, address autocomplete, phone with a country-code dropdown, password rules with confirmation, consent boxes, radio "other" text, custom date pickers, contenteditable, nested shadow DOM, an iframe, fields revealed by a selection, async username checks, CSRF/hidden fields, chip inputs, button-and-listbox dropdowns, and seven tasks that must be refused (CAPTCHA, wrong format, server rejection, disabled control, unknown field, terms that stay disabled, username taken). Nothing is scraped; the pages are written from knowledge of those patterns.

Every task has a ground-truth final state, and success is judged by **what the fixture server received**, never by what the tool said. A wrong value, or a "Submitted" that the server did not see, is a *wrong-fill*; the suite exits non-zero on any.

| run | pass | correctly refused | failed honestly | wrong-fills |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| first run, 27 tasks, before fixes | 17 | 6 | 3 | **1** |
| after fixes, 30 tasks | 23 | 7 | 0 | 0 |

Read that honestly: the suite was written by the people who fixed what it found, so 30/30 is a regression floor, not a claim about the open web. The first run is the informative one: a bare day number (`5`) matched the options 05, 15 and 25 and was refused as ambiguous; an address suggestion list that shows the full address could not be picked by its street; inputs inside nested shadow roots were split into separate forms with no submit button; and an array sent to a chip-style combobox was typed into the box as text and reported *Verified* while nothing had been chosen (the wrong-fill). The tests that guard these are in `crates/ostler-browser/tests/suite_regressions_e2e.rs`.

```sh
./target/release/ostler-bench suite                # whole suite; --only <text> for one task; --json out/suite.json
OSTLER_SUITE_TRANSCRIPT=1 ./target/release/ostler-bench suite --only chip   # print the tool output for non-passing tasks
```

## 7. Real-site evaluation (fill only, no LLM)

`ostler-bench real` opens seven live public form-practice pages (demoqa's practice form, formy, practice-automation, selenium.dev's `web-form.html`, testpages.eviltester, expandtesting's register page, ultimateqa's contact page), calls `form_inspect` then `form_fill`, and then reads **45 fields back out of the page with our own JavaScript**, never from the tool's report. It does **not** submit: these are other people's servers.

Every field ends in one of three states: **ok** (the page holds the expected value), **flagged** (it does not, and the fill report said so: `UNMATCHED`, `FAILED`, a warning naming the key), or **false claim** (it does not, and the report did not say so). False claims are the number that has to be zero. The run exits non-zero on any.

| run | fields ok | flagged | false claims | slowest `navigate` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| first run | 42 / 44 | 0 | **2** | 38.7 s |
| after the two fixes below | 44 / 45 | 1 | **0** | 14.0 s |

The one flagged field is a deliberate probe: a key (`Favourite colour of the moon`) that matches nothing on the page. The report says `UNMATCHED key … no field on the page matches this key`. The same page's disabled and read-only inputs are asked to change; both keep their value and both are reported (`is disabled on this page`, `is read-only`).

What the first run found, and what changed:

1. **A silent tie between forms.** `ultimateqa.com/filling-out-forms/` has two forms that both have a `Name` and a `Message`. Ostler filled the *later* one (the one with a CAPTCHA question) and said `Filled 2/2`. Nothing on the page was wrong, but the agent was never told there was a choice. A tie now goes to the first form in the document, and the report says `WARNING: 1 other form(s) on this page matched these keys equally well (e15); this filled form e11. Pass form=<ref> to choose another.` (`fill.rs`, regression test `two_forms_that_match_equally_fill_the_first_and_name_the_other`).
2. **`navigate` waited for the `load` event, up to 30 s.** `load` waits for every image, ad and tracker. `practice.expandtesting.com` took 31.7 s to open and `practice-automation.com` 38.7 s, while the form was usable in under a second (the latter's server itself needs 6.5 s to answer). Now, once the new document is interactive, `load` gets 5 more seconds and Ostler carries on, telling the agent so (`page was still loading images or scripts 5s after it became usable; continuing`). Those two pages now open in 7.5 s and 14.0 s. The same cap applies to clicks that navigate. A fixture with a stalled image guards it (`a_stalled_subresource_does_not_hold_navigation_for_the_whole_timeout`).

Per-call time on these pages: `form_inspect` 4 to 25 ms, `form_fill` 68 to 385 ms. Opening the page is the cost, as on every browser tool.

**What this does not show.** The corpus is small, and the pages are *practice* pages built to be automated; they are friendlier than a bank, a government portal or a checkout behind a bot wall. The fill values and the DOM checks were written by us after looking at each form, so this is a check that the engine's claims match the page, not a held-out test of success on the open web. There is no model in the loop and no comparison with another tool. Sites change or disappear: a page that cannot be loaded is reported `unreachable` and left out of the rates. Do not quote 98% as a success rate on real websites.

```sh
./target/release/ostler-bench real                 # needs network; --only <text> for one site; --json out/real.json
OSTLER_REAL_TRANSCRIPT=1 ./target/release/ostler-bench real --only selenium   # print the tool output
```

## 8. Reproduce

```sh
cargo build --release -p ostler-bench -p ostler
./target/release/ostler-bench --json out/forms.json forms --reps 3
./target/release/ostler-bench --json out/footprint.json footprint
./target/release/ostler-bench --json out/concurrency.json concurrency --sessions 1,2,4,8 --lean
OSTLER_QDRANT_BIN=/path/to/qdrant ./target/release/ostler-bench --json out/memory.json memory --sizes 1000x20,10000x20
scripts/bench-compare.sh          # section 5: builds, npm-installs the pinned competitors in a temp dir, runs, writes bench-results/compare.{json,md}
# Cost knobs: --price-in --price-out --llm-turn-secs --base-context   (forms)
#             --vcpu-hour-usd --gib-hour-usd                          (concurrency)
```

Raw results from the run documented here are in [`bench-results/`](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/tree/main/bench-results). The `bench` GitHub workflow re-runs these on Linux runners and uploads artifacts, which also gives PSS-based memory numbers.

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/ostler-vs-playwright-mcp.html

# Ostler vs Playwright MCP

Playwright MCP and Ostler are both MCP servers that give an agent a browser, and both have a batched form-fill tool. On five scripted form tasks on local fixtures, both finished every task correctly; Ostler used fewer tool calls (19 against 27) and Playwright MCP's tool list is larger. No language model was in the loop, no real website was used, and the numbers say nothing about which tool a real agent will complete tasks with more often. Choose on the differences below, not on the step counts alone.

## Where they differ

| | Ostler | Playwright MCP |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Local Rust binary that runs Chrome and serves MCP and A2A. Early: v0.2, development source, no tagged release. | Microsoft's MCP server for Playwright, installed from npm. Mature and broad. |
| Form filling | `form_fill` takes a label-to-value map, then reads every value back from the live page and reports mismatches. `form_submit` is a separate step with its own outcome. | `browser_fill_form` fills several fields in one call from a page snapshot. |
| Research | `read`, `cite` and `evidence` check quotations against pages read in the session and report pages that could not be read. See [research with checked citations](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/research-with-citations.html). | Reads pages as accessibility snapshots. This project did not evaluate it for quotation checking, so no claim is made either way. |
| Memory | Optional, in your own Qdrant: saved facts and per-site playbooks. See [memory and privacy](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/memory.html). | Browser profile only. |
| Tool list size | 21 tools in the tested version, about 1,513 estimated tokens of definitions. Today's full list is 32 tools in five profiles; the default `auto` profile starts with 15. | 25 tools, about 5,265 estimated tokens of definitions. |
| Platforms | Chrome or Chromium; tested on macOS locally and Linux in CI. Windows and Docker are experimental and arrive in v0.2.1. | See Playwright MCP's own documentation. |

The Ostler column is from this project's own documentation. For Playwright MCP, the only facts used here are the ones this project measured on the version below; check its documentation for anything else.

## What was measured

Scripted, model-free, five tasks on local fixtures. A deterministic script plays the shortest sensible tool sequence for each server, using each server's own batch-fill tool, and every task is judged by what the fixture server received, not by what the tool said.

| | Ostler | Playwright MCP |
|---|---|---|
| Version tested | 0.2.0 (the revision was not recorded; see below) | `@playwright/mcp` 0.0.84 (reports Playwright 1.65.0-alpha-2026-10-30), `--headless --isolated --browser chrome` |
| Tasks completed correctly | 5 of 5 | 5 of 5 |
| Tool calls, all five tasks | 19 | 27 |
| Output tokens, all five tasks (bytes / 4, an estimate) | 1,550 | 2,960 |
| Tool time, all five tasks | 4.1 s | 8.8 s |

Per task, tool calls (Ostler against Playwright MCP): basic form 3 against 4, validation 3 against 4, dependent dropdowns 3 against 5, three-step wizard 7 against 10, 20-field form 3 against 4.

Conditions: 2026-11-02, Apple M2, macOS 26.6, one machine over localhost, headless, Google Chrome 156.0.8078.74, Node v26.10.0, median of 3 runs per task. The Chrome DevTools MCP server was measured in the same run and is in the [benchmarks](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html#5-ostler-vs-playwright-mcp-vs-chrome-devtools-mcp-same-fixtures-scripted-agent).

## What this does not show

- **No language model.** A real model may take more or fewer steps than the scripted ideal. The script gives every server its best case.
- **Fixtures only.** Five tasks on local pages. None of the hostile behaviours in the other fixtures (CAPTCHA, shadow DOM, comboboxes, rich inputs) were run against Playwright MCP, so how it handles them is not measured here.
- **Correctness is a tie.** All three servers completed every task correctly in every run. The read-back that Ostler adds is what lets an agent detect a silent failure, but these fixtures never triggered one, so its value is not measured here.
- **Ostler is not always cheaper.** On small forms Chrome DevTools MCP returned fewer output tokens than Ostler, because Ostler's replies carry the read-back text. The step gap against batch-fill tools is about 1.4 times, not the larger gap seen against one call per field.
- **Wall time is not end-to-end latency.** Differences of a few hundred milliseconds are well under one model turn.
- **Versions move.** Playwright MCP has changed how navigation returns snapshots between releases. The sequences are this project's best attempt for each server and were not reviewed by its authors. A shorter sequence would change the numbers.
- **The Ostler revision was not recorded.** The raw results record the version string `ostler 0.2.0` and the date, not a commit. `git log` of the repository gives the history of the documents, not the revision that was measured.

The larger headline gaps elsewhere on this site (3 calls against 22 on a 20-field form, 13 times fewer input tokens) compare Ostler's form engine with the same engine driven one field per call. That is not a measurement of Playwright MCP.

## When to choose which

- **Choose Playwright MCP** if you need a mature, widely used tool, you want the documentation and ecosystem around Playwright, or you need a platform Ostler does not support. For simple, small forms the two tools are close.
- **Choose Ostler** if the agent must report what actually ended up in each field, if your workflow needs checked quotations and an explicit list of pages it could not read, or if you want per-site form memory in your own Qdrant. Accept that it is early software without a tagged release and without real-site success rates.
- **Choose neither on this page's evidence alone.** Run your own task. The harness is in the repository: `scripts/bench-compare.sh` reproduces the table above, and the [benchmark methods](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html#8-reproduce) list every flag.

## Reproduce it

```sh
scripts/bench-compare.sh    # builds, installs the pinned competitors in a temp dir, writes bench-results/compare.{json,md}
```

Raw data: [`bench-results/compare.json`](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/bench-results/compare.json) and [`compare.md`](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/blob/main/bench-results/compare.md). If you find a shorter sequence for either server, please [open an issue](https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler/issues).


---

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/economics.html

# Economics and scale: the hard questions

Written as the questions a skeptical investor or senior engineer would ask, answered with what we measured ([BENCHMARKS.md](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html)) and clearly separated from what we assume. Where we do not know, we say so.

## 1. What does one task cost, and who pays for what?

For a typical form task (measured on fixtures; LLM price is an illustrative $3 / $15 per Mtok):

| cost line | per task | share | basis |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| LLM tokens (3 calls, prompt-cached) | ~$0.017-0.024 | **>99%** | measured token counts x illustrative price |
| Browser compute | ~$0.000006 | ~0.03% | measured 0.5 CPU-s + 0.5 GiB for ~1 s, illustrative cloud price |
| Qdrant (memory ops) | ~2 requests, sub-ms | negligible | measured; Cloud Inference model cost not measured |

**Implication:** the browser is not the cost center, the model is. A browser that is 2x faster or cheaper to run changes the bill by nothing. A browser that makes the agent take fewer turns and read fewer tokens changes it a lot: on a 20-field form we measure **5.0x lower LLM cost and 5.4x lower latency** than a per-field interaction pattern. Ostler's economic claim is therefore "fewer turns and fewer tokens per completed form", not "faster browser".

## 2. Is the saving real, or an artefact of the baseline?

Partly baseline. The "per-field" comparison models the worst-case pattern (one call per field, full snapshot after each). Tools with batched fills close part of the gap. What stays differentiated even against a batched filler: verification by read-back, dependent dropdown/wizard handling in one call, shadow DOM/iframes, validation-error reporting, and cross-session memory. We do not yet have a head-to-head against other products on the same tasks; that is on the roadmap and we will publish it either way.

## 3. How does it scale?

**Per node (measured, 8-core laptop):** 8 parallel sessions gave 354-393 tasks/min, p95 under 1 s, 100% success, flat latency, 450-550 MiB per session. Derived planning numbers, assuming CPU-bound at 0.5 CPU-s per task: ~7,000 tasks per core-hour; memory-bound at ~0.5 GiB per session: ~14 concurrent sessions per 8 GB, ~120 per 64 GB. Assumptions: Linux numbers will differ; real sites are heavier than fixtures (more CPU, more RAM per page); idle sessions hold memory. Treat as a first-order estimate until the Linux benchmark job reports.

**Memory layer (measured on real Qdrant):** retrieval latency stays ~0.4 ms p50 from 20k to 200k points because queries are tenant-scoped via a payload index. Throughput ~2.4-2.9k QPS with 16 clients on one laptop-hosted node.

**What does not scale yet (be skeptical here):**
- Qdrant RAM per user is the open number. We saw ~6.8-8.4 KB per point at 200k points untuned, i.e. ~130-160 KB per user at 20 facts. At 1M users that is ~130-160 GB untuned. It is a loaded-and-queried figure, not isolated steady state, so it is an upper-ish bound, but it needs a proper sizing study with quantization and on-disk vectors before any capacity claim.
- Hosted multi-tenant browsers (isolation, anti-abuse, residential proxies, CAPTCHAs) are not built and are where hosted-browser companies spend most of their cost.

## 4. What are the unit economics of a business around this?

This repository is an open-source tool (Apache-2.0), not a business. The plausible shapes, with their honest weaknesses:

1. **Pull-through for Qdrant Cloud.** Each active user holds a small memory footprint and issues a few queries per form. Value to Qdrant is adoption and a reference workload, not direct revenue per user (the volume per user is small). *Weakness:* low revenue per seat.
2. **Hosted sessions** (managed browsers with memory). Compute is cheap (section 1), so gross margin is high before proxies, CAPTCHAs and abuse handling, which is where margin disappears. *Weakness:* crowded, and the hard costs are the ones we have not built.
3. **Enterprise** (audit log, policy, SSO, approval workflows, on-prem). *Weakness:* needs real-site reliability evidence first.

We do not put revenue numbers here because we have no basis for them.

## 5. What is the moat?

Honest answer: **not the language, not the browser.** agent-browser (Vercel) is already a native Rust CLI with MCP and ~45k stars; Rust is table stakes. What can compound:
- **Per-user memory** (playbooks, profile, known issues) is switching cost and quality that improves with use.
- **A form corpus**: fingerprints of forms and which strategies worked. Opt-in, anonymised cross-user sharing is a possible network effect, and a privacy risk that must be designed in from the start (not built).
- **Published, reproducible benchmarks** that others have to match.

What can erode it: competitors adding memory (it is not hard in principle), and model vendors shipping first-party browser agents that need no external tool.

## 6. What can go wrong?

| risk | status |
|---|---|
| Real-site success rate unknown (we test fixtures only) | **Biggest gap, partly addressed.** `ostler-bench real` fills 7 live practice pages and checks every field against the DOM: 44 of 45 correct, 0 false claims after two fixes ([BENCHMARKS §7](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html#7-real-site-evaluation-fill-only-no-llm)). Small and friendly; a wider real-model evaluation is still the next milestone. |
| Computer-use models make DOM tooling less necessary | Real. Forms with consent/legal gates still want structured, verifiable filling; unproven. |
| Anti-bot, CAPTCHA, SSO/2FA, cross-origin iframes | Not handled (documented limitations). |
| Memory leaks PII or is poisoned by a malicious page | Mitigated: secrets refused at write, sensitive fields never auto-filled or stored, values not stored in playbooks, tenant isolation tested, page content marked untrusted. Not a security audit. |
| Qdrant Cloud Inference path untested live | The request shape follows Qdrant's docs and is pinned by tests, but no live cluster was available. Everything else is tested against a real Qdrant server. |
| Benchmark credibility | One machine, fixtures, illustrative prices. Raw data, harness, flags and caveats are published; Linux CI job adds a second platform. |

## 7. Test matrix (what is covered and how)

| aspect | what we test | where | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Correctness** | Browser e2e tests (`forms_e2e.rs`, `security_e2e.rs`; 56 and 10 `#[tokio::test]` functions when checked) assert on what the *server received*: dependent dropdowns, wizard, controlled inputs, masks, comboboxes, shadow DOM, iframes, dates/times/files, 20-field form, validation errors | `crates/ostler-browser/tests` | passing |
| **Form logic** | key->field matching (ambiguity reported, never guessed), option/date/time normalisation, sensitive-field detection, fingerprints | `ostler-forms` unit tests (14) | passing |
| **Protocol** | real binary over MCP stdio: initialize, tools, memory learning loop, confirm gate, domain policy, profiles | `crates/ostler-cli/tests` | passing |
| **Memory** | store semantics on a real Qdrant: roundtrip, isolation, upsert, dimension mismatch, 20 concurrent tenants; sealed payloads and tenant tokens on a real Qdrant (`sealed_real.rs`, `tenant_token_real.rs`); Cloud Inference request shape via mock | `ostler-memory` tests (11 + 3 real) | passing |
| **Cost** | tool calls and tokens per task, LLM cost model (unit-tested) | `ostler-bench forms`, `cost.rs` tests | measured |
| **Latency** | per-task tool time, cold start; regression found and fixed (3 s to 160 ms) | bench + e2e | measured |
| **Scale** | parallel sessions, memory per session, CPU per task, Qdrant at 200k points | `ostler-bench concurrency/memory/footprint` | measured (one machine) |
| **Context cost** | tool schema size capped by a unit test (under 7 KB) | `ostler-mcp` tests | enforced |
| **Security** | domain allowlist (suffix-attack cases), scheme blocking, confirm gate, secret refusal, untrusted-content marking | policy + MCP tests | passing; no external audit |
| **Not yet covered** | real-site success rate; Linux/Windows; cross-origin iframes; long-running leak soak; Cloud Inference live; fuzzing the JSON-RPC layer | roadmap | open |

## 8. What would change our minds

If the real-site evaluation shows success rates no better than existing tools, the form engine is not a differentiator and the project's value reduces to the memory integration. If Qdrant memory per user cannot be brought under a few tens of KB with quantization and on-disk storage, the "memory for everyone" story needs a smaller unit (store less, or share more).


---

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/review.html

# Design review, 2026-10-30 (v0.2.0)

Five independent read-only reviews: form engine, Qdrant memory, MCP/security, CDP/lifecycle, benchmarks/claims. 74 findings in total; this page keeps the ones that matter, grouped by the design flaw they share. "C" = confirmed from the code path, "S" = suspected. No reviewer reproduced issues live; all 73 tests pass, which mostly says the tests miss these cases.

## Status

Updated as work lands. **Fixed** means there is a regression test that fails without the change.

| finding | status |
|---|---|
| Ambiguous key wins by elimination after rivals are filled | **fixed** (keys resolve against all visible fields) |
| Form re-mounted mid-fill abandons keys; `ok()` ignored unmatched keys | **fixed**; also follows stale refs by label for read-back |
| Memory: playbook key cut at first space | **fixed** (structured provenance) |
| Memory: one accepted semantic guess becomes a permanent 0.95 rule | **fixed** (only playbook/autocomplete matches persist) |
| Memory: `--learn` overwrites user facts | **fixed** (`Memory::learn` never replaces a non-learned fact) |
| Memory: semantic top-1 with no margin; "spouse/emergency" labels | **fixed** (margin 0.05; other-person labels never use semantic) |
| Secrets in notes, snapshots, episodes | **fixed** (notes hidden, snapshot masks, episodes scrubbed of typed values and long digit runs) |
| Untrusted wrapper escapable; reports/titles unwrapped | **fixed** (defanged; reports wrapped; titles, URLs, dialog text and the `look` legend are now quarantined too, found by a prompt-injection page in the 2026-10-31 soak) |
| Allowlist checked after the fact | **fixed** for every request type and WebSockets (catch-all interception plus a browser-wide resolver rule; verified with a canary server). Ports are still ignored |
| Tools skip the policy check | **fixed** for snapshot, inspect, fill, submit, screenshot |
| `--require-confirm-submit` only guards `form_submit` | **fixed** (all non-GET requests blocked outside a confirmed submit) |
| Dead Chrome never relaunched; first call waits a timeout | **fixed** |
| `panic = "abort"` defeats Chrome cleanup | **fixed** (removed) |
| WebSocket frame limit kills the connection | **fixed** (limits raised) |
| Popups unseen and unpoliced | **fixed** (popups become tabs under the same policy) |
| Tool output bloat | **fixed**: terse by default, `--verbose` for detail |
| Upload of any local path | **fixed** (refused unless `--upload-dir`; paths resolved so `..` and symlinks cannot escape) |
| DevTools TCP port reachable by local users (use `--remote-debugging-pipe`) | **fixed** (pipe transport by default; verified no listening socket; `OSTLER_CDP_TRANSPORT=ws` is the old behaviour) |
| Default policy permits loopback/private/metadata addresses; ports ignored | **partly fixed**: `--block-private-networks` (default on for `a2a`) and `host:port` allowlist entries. `serve` with no allowlist is still open by default; DNS rebinding can outwit the name check |
| `confirm()` auto-accepted | **fixed** (`confirm`/`prompt` dismissed unless `--accept-dialogs`) |
| Chrome orphaned on SIGKILL/SIGTERM of the server | **fixed on the pipe transport** (Chrome exits when the pipe closes; the temp profile directory of a SIGKILLed server is still left behind) |
| Submit classification, error attribution, settle on busy pages, O(n^2) re-scan, isolated world, refs reused across documents | open |
| Combobox async options; some widgets (MUI select, read-only Ant select, cross-origin iframes) | open |
| Qdrant: short deadline + circuit breaker, `forget` cascade, episode TTL, tenant auth, `hnsw m:0`, model-name check | open |
| Benchmarks: no LLM in the loop, strawman baseline, no batched-tool baselines | labels corrected; the real evaluation is **open** |

## The five design flaws

### 1. "Never guess" is not actually enforced: wrong fills can be reported as Verified (critical)

The project's central promise is that ambiguity is reported, not guessed. Several paths break it.

| where | flaw | |
|---|---|---|
| `fill.rs:227-236` | Keys are re-resolved every round against the *remaining* fields, so a key reported ambiguous in round 1 wins by elimination in round 2 (`"phone"` lands in Shipping phone). | C |
| `fill.rs:217-223, 292-295` | If the framework re-mounts the `<form>` mid-fill, `pick_form` returns None, the report block is skipped, and pending keys vanish with `ok() == true`. | C |
| `memory/lib.rs:479-492`, `app.rs:151` | Semantic recall takes top-1 over an absolute threshold, with no margin, no type check, no "someone else" guard (spouse/reference/emergency). Auto-fill of required fields is the default when memory is on. | C (scores S) |
| `app.rs:662-666` | Any memory-sourced fill on an accepted submit becomes a 0.95-confidence playbook mapping, so one wrong guess is replayed forever. | C |
| `app.rs:665` | Playbook key parsed with `split_whitespace().next()`: "Email address" is stored as "Email", "work email" as "work". | C (bug) |
| `app.rs:748-752` | `--learn` upserts page-labelled facts over user-entered facts; a "refer a friend: Email" form overwrites the user's email. | C |
| `fill.rs:536-551`, `page.rs:500-512` | Native-setter fallback verifies immediately with no settle; frameworks revert later. `type_into` ignores `focused:false`, so text can land in another field. No final re-verify pass. | C |
| `runtime.js:690-704`, `fill.rs:771-779` | Combobox picks the first visible options (stale async results), falls back to any `[role=option]` on the page, accepts one-way substring hits; verification treats "United States Minor Outlying Islands" ≈ "United States". | C |
| `fill.rs:799`, `runtime.js:430` | `datetime-local` always verifies; value-less radios all read "on". | C |

**Design fix:** resolve all keys once against the full field list and freeze the result; make memory suggestions advisory unless top-1 has a margin and a type match; learn mappings only from user/agent-provided values; a final settle + re-verify pass over every result.

### 2. The safety model is checked after the browser has acted (high)

| where | flaw | |
|---|---|---|
| `page.rs:278-378`, `policy.rs` | The allowlist is checked at navigate start and after actions. No `Fetch` interception, so cross-origin form actions, redirects, page fetch/XHR, beacons and iframes reach forbidden origins first. | C |
| `app.rs:343-536` | `snapshot`, `form_inspect`, `form_fill`, `screenshot`, `wait_for` skip the policy check; a delayed redirect gets the agent's (and memory's) values typed into a forbidden page. | C |
| `app.rs:705` | `--require-confirm-submit` is only on `form_submit`. `click` on the submit button, `type submit:true`, `press Enter`, or page JS on change/blur all submit. | C |
| `fill.rs:483`, `page.rs:598` | File fields accept any local path (`~/.ssh/id_rsa`); errors reveal which files exist. | C |
| `app.rs:168`, `runtime.js:233` | The `<page_content untrusted>` wrapper is not escaped, and fill/submit reports, titles and dialog text are not wrapped at all. | C |
| `launch.rs:117` | The DevTools TCP port is reachable by any local user; with `--profile-dir` that is the user's logged-in browser. SECURITY.md understates this. | C |
| `policy.rs:27-30` | An empty allowlist permits loopback, LAN and 169.254.169.254; entries ignore ports. | C |
| `launch.rs:131` | `--disable-popup-blocking` with no target auto-attach: popups load unpoliced and unseen. | C |
| `page.rs:154-168` | Every `confirm()` is auto-accepted, including a site's own "really pay?" check. | C |

**Design fix:** enforce in the browser, not the tool layer: `Fetch.enable` to block disallowed document/subframe requests and to hold submit-triggered navigations for confirmation; `Target.setAutoAttach`; `--remote-debugging-pipe`; private ranges blocked by default; uploads off unless `--upload-dir`.

### 3. Secrets leak through side channels (medium-high)

Masking covers `requested`/`observed` only. Leaks: the `note` field (Mismatch and NoMatch embed raw values, `fill.rs:715`, `values.rs:81`); snapshots show `value=` for sensitive non-password inputs (`runtime.js:255`); episodes store page validation text that echoes values, never filtered and not removed by `forget` (`app.rs:758-766`). `looks_sensitive` is substring-based: it blocks `shipping_address` ("pin") and misses passports and card numbers inside text. `forget` does not cascade; Qdrant WAL and snapshots keep data.

### 4. The browser layer has no recovery and almost no tests (high)

- A dead Chrome is never relaunched: every later call fails until the MCP process restarts (`app.rs:247-256`, `cdp/lib.rs:85-119`). C
- A single oversized frame (a tall full-page screenshot over tungstenite's limits) ends the reader loop permanently (`cdp/lib.rs:85`). S
- Chrome and the temp profile are left behind on SIGTERM or panic. v0.2 had added `panic = "abort"`, which stopped `kill_on_drop` from running (`launch.rs:150`). C. **Reverted** after this review; signal handling is still missing.
- Navigation detection uses a 180 ms window plus a bare load counter: late navigations are missed and stale load events satisfy later waits; the `navigate` timeout is discarded (`page.rs:290-345`). C
- Eval retries on context loss can run side effects twice (`page.rs:180-230`). S
- No tests for the CDP client, lifecycle or navigation logic. C

### 5. The evidence does not support the headline yet (critical for credibility)

- No LLM in the loop: both modes are a fixed script with hard-coded labels (`forms.rs:28-178`). C
- The per-field baseline is weakened: `observe:"full"` plus an extra full snapshot after every field, while Ostler's own tools default to delta (`forms.rs:315, 329`). C
- The batched-fill competitors (Playwright MCP `browser_fill_form`, chrome-devtools-mcp `fill_form`) are not run, and the README misdescribes chrome-devtools-mcp as debugging-only. C
- "5.4x faster" is `turns x 3 s`: the call-count ratio restated, presented as "measured". C
- A 1.5k-token base context is unrealistic for coding agents; at 20k the 20-field cost ratio drops from ~5x to ~2.7x. C
- The headline is the best case (20 fields); the 9-scenario aggregate is 1.7x, and combobox is 1.0x. "Median of 3" applies to tool time only. C
- The memory benchmark uses hash vectors, 20 identical points per tenant, no wait for indexing, a single RSS sample: "flat at 200k" is true by construction. The Qdrant multitenancy setup is missing `hnsw_config {m:0, payload_m:16}`. C
- Stagehand's action caching is a shipped equivalent of playbooks; the moat section ignores it. C

## Other notable findings

- Form-less pages: all controls become one "page" form whose submit candidates are document-wide; `SUBMIT_RE` matches "search"/"go", so the header search button can be clicked (`runtime.js:507-552`). Any type-less `<button>` counts as submit (`runtime.js:468`). C
- Submit classification: a confirmation page that has any input is "Advanced"; XHR success with the form still present is "Unchanged"; `hidden` is never set, so its check is dead code (`fill.rs:648-663`). C
- Error attribution searches the grandparent, so one invalid field's message is attached to its neighbours; `.help-block` counts as an error (`runtime.js:370-376`). C
- Settle never settles on pages with polling, streaming or animation, and the result is ignored; each round re-walks the whole DOM, making fills O(n²) (`runtime.js:32-44, 764-779`). C
- Runtime lives in the page world (`window.__wm`, wrapped `fetch`/`setTimeout` visible to bot detection); should use an isolated world. S
- Refs restart at `e1` per document and the refs Map never frees (`runtime.js:51-58`). C
- Qdrant: 10 s timeout × up to 4 sequential requests per field, errors swallowed, with no "memory degraded" signal (`qdrant.rs:56`, `app.rs:486`); tenant is an unauthenticated string defaulting to "default"; model changes with the same dimension go undetected. C
- JSON-RPC: the empty batch gets no error, batch replies are not an array, requests are strictly sequential, so a 60 s `wait_for` blocks `ping`; cancellation is ignored. C
- Blocking `ps`/`footprint` calls inside async code while holding the browser mutex (`launch.rs:220, 277`). C

## Recommended order of work

1. **Stop wrong fills** (flaw 1): freeze key resolution, gate memory suggestions, fix the playbook key bug, never overwrite user facts, final re-verify. Each comes with a fixture that currently passes wrongly.
2. **Add browser relaunch** (`panic = "abort"` already reverted), signal handling and `--remote-debugging-pipe` (flaw 4, plus part of flaw 2).
3. **Browser-level enforcement** of allowlist, confirm gate and uploads; escape and extend the untrusted wrapper; mask notes and snapshots (flaws 2, 3).
4. **Honest benchmarks**: add batched/delta baselines, a realistic base context, and "modelled" labels now; then an LLM-in-the-loop eval against real Playwright MCP / chrome-devtools-mcp / agent-browser, plus a held-out real-site set (flaw 5). Update the README and site until then.

Source: https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/troubleshooting.html

# Troubleshooting

Start with `ostler doctor`. It launches Chrome, round-trips a page and, if memory is on, prints a memory report and checks Qdrant. The report says in plain words what is stored where and what leaves the machine:

```text
Memory: on, Qdrant at https://… (tenant "default")
  sealing:    ON … (or OFF, with a warning)
  key:        <path to memory.key> (owner-only, good)   | from OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY | not created yet
  embeddings: cloud | local (ollama at …) | local dev-hash
  isolation:  shared collections | one set of collections per tenant
  transport:  https (encrypted) | http to this machine | http to a remote host: REFUSED / ALLOWED
  qdrant:     reachable, collections ready. OK
```

With nothing configured it prints `Memory: in-process, this session only` and the rest still works. It never creates the sealing key. Every failing check prints a `fix:` line with a concrete command. `ostler doctor --fix` applies only the safe ones: it creates the config directory and tightens an over-open key file to owner-only. It never creates keys, installs software, edits client configs or touches the network. `ostler doctor --cdp-url http://127.0.0.1:9222` also tests attaching to a Chrome you started yourself.

| symptom | likely cause | fix |
|---|---|---|
| `serve --cdp-url` says it could not read `/json/version` | no Chrome is listening on that port, or it was started without a dedicated `--user-data-dir` (Chrome ignores the debug flag on its default profile) | start it as in [CLIENTS.md](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/agents.html#use-the-chrome-you-already-have), then `ostler doctor --cdp-url ...` |
| `--cdp-url ... refusing a non-loopback host` | the URL points off this machine | use 127.0.0.1; for a remote browser tunnel the port with SSH |
| `ostler install` says the file is not valid JSON/TOML | the client's config has a typo or comments | nothing was written; fix the file, or add the snippet from `ostler setup <client>` by hand |
| Client says it can't start `ostler` / command not found | the client has a different `PATH` than your shell | use `ostler setup <client>`, which writes the binary's **absolute path** |
| `Chrome: could not find Chrome or Chromium` | none on the usual paths | install one (the message has the command for your OS), or set `OSTLER_CHROME=/path/to/chrome` |
| `the Chrome path "…" does not exist` | `OSTLER_CHROME` or `--chrome-path` points at a missing file | fix the path, or unset it to auto-detect (a wrong explicit path is an error on purpose, never silently replaced) |
| Launch fails with "exited before DevTools was ready" on Linux/Docker | running as root, or no sandbox support | set `OSTLER_NO_SANDBOX=1`; in containers also give Chrome a larger `/dev/shm` (`--shm-size=1g`) |
| The first call after Chrome crashed reports a restart | the server relaunches Chrome and tells the agent; open tabs and page state are lost | re-navigate and continue; if it keeps failing, restart the MCP server (in Claude Code: `/mcp`, reconnect) |
| Server prints nothing and the agent sees no tools | stdout must carry only MCP messages; something else wrote to it, or the client expects another transport | run `ostler serve` in a terminal: it should print one `ready` line on stderr and wait |
| `form_fill` says `UNMATCHED key` | no field label/name matches that key | call `form_inspect`, then pass the exact label or the `eNN` ref |
| `ambiguous` in a fill report | several fields match equally well | use the ref (`e12`) from `form_inspect` instead of a label |
| `NOT ACCEPTED` with the page's message | the page rejected the values | fix the named fields and call `form_submit` again |
| `sealing: OFF. warning: anyone who can read your Qdrant ...` | `--seal off` (or `seal = off` in the config) | `ostler config set seal on`, then `ostler memory seal` to protect facts saved earlier (learned skills and episodes from before are dropped and relearned) |
| `warning: other users on this machine can read the key` | `memory.key` is not owner-only | `chmod 600` on the path doctor prints |
| the sealing key is unreadable or malformed, or sealed memory returns nothing | `memory.key` / `OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY` is missing, damaged or a different key than the one that sealed it | restore your backup to the path doctor names. **There is no recovery without the key**: delete the key file and run `ostler memory wipe --yes` to start over. Points that fail to open are skipped, never returned |
| `refusing to create a new memory key` | no key exists yet and Qdrant could not be checked (or holds sealed memory this machine has no key for) | start Qdrant and retry; restore a backup with `ostler memory key import`; for a genuine first-time setup with Qdrant down pass `--allow-new-key`. If sealed memory is there and the key is gone, `ostler memory wipe --yes` starts over |
| `retired sealed format v1` or `older key normalisation` | sealed points from an early build, or keys saved before `norm()` changed | `ostler memory seal --tenant T` (the key is right; this brings the data up to date) |
| `refusing plain http` / `transport: http to a remote host: REFUSED` | the Qdrant URL is plain `http://` to a non-loopback host, so the API key and any unsealed data would cross the network in clear text | use an `https://` URL; if a VPN or SSH tunnel protects the link, pass `--allow-insecure-qdrant` (`ostler config set allow_insecure_qdrant true`) |
| `warning: Cloud Inference only exists on Qdrant Cloud, and this URL is not one` | `--embeddings cloud` (the default) with a self-hosted URL | `--embeddings ollama` (semantic, local) or `dev-hash` (local, not semantic) |
| `cannot reach the local embedder` / embedding model not found | `--embeddings ollama` but Ollama is not running, or the model is not pulled | `ollama serve`, `ollama pull all-minilm` (the Ollama default), or `ostler config set embedding_model <name>` and `embedding_dim` to match |
| `warning: model "…/…" looks like a Qdrant Cloud model name` | an Ollama setup still carrying the Cloud default model | `ostler config set embedding_model all-minilm` |
| `Qdrant rejected the API key` (401/403) with `--isolation collection` | a scoped token only covers its own tenant's collections | use the token from `ostler memory token` for the same `--tenant`; Qdrant must run with `service.jwt_rbac: true` and an admin must have created the collections first (`ostler memory list` as admin does it) |
| `this collection was created with a different embedding model` | the collection's vector size does not match `--embedding-model` / `--embedding-dim` | use the same model as before, or a different tenant or cluster |
| `SERVER ERROR: the site answered with an HTTP error` from `form_submit` | the submit got a 4xx/5xx and the page showed no validation messages | the data may or may not have been stored: do not retry blindly; check with `snapshot` or ask the user |
| `2 forms on this page and none was filled: pass form (...)` | `form_submit` with several forms and no `form` or `control`, and no earlier `form_fill` on this page | pass the form ref from `form_inspect`, or a submit `control` ref |
| `qdrant:     FAILED` in doctor | wrong `QDRANT_URL`/key, or Cloud Inference not enabled on the cluster | doctor prints a specific fix (unreachable, rejected key, or embedding-size mismatch). Check the URL includes the port (`:6333`), enable Inference in the Qdrant Cloud console, or use `--embeddings ollama` (local, semantic) or `--embeddings dev-hash` (not semantic) against open-source Qdrant. Memory is optional: unset `QDRANT_URL` to run without it |
| A tool result starts with `Note: memory is unavailable (...)` | Qdrant failed twice in a row (down, slow past the 4 s request limit, or returning 5xx); lookups are skipped for 30 s, then one request retries | the form tools keep working: pass values in the request. Fix Qdrant (`ostler doctor`), no restart needed |
| `... is a cloud metadata address (always blocked ...)` | the agent tried 169.254.169.254, `fe80::/10` or `metadata.google.internal` | intended. If you really need it, add it to `--allow-domain` |
| A submit comes back as `Nothing changed` on a page that stays put | the site posts in the background and says nothing visible afterwards, so Ostler cannot tell it worked | check with `snapshot`; do not resubmit blindly (it may have gone through) |
| `npx -y ostler …` is slow the first time, or fails offline | the launcher downloads the binary once (cached in `~/.cache/ostler`) | run `npx -y ostler doctor` once while online; or install the binary with `pip install ostler-mcp` / `install.sh` and point your client at it (the npm package is not published yet) |
| `checksum mismatch … Not installing` | the download was corrupted or altered | nothing was installed or run. Retry; if it persists, install from source and open an issue |
| Agent context fills up | too many tools or large snapshots | `--tools forms`, `--lean`, and ask for `form_inspect` instead of full `snapshot` |
| A tool result starts with `CHALLENGE:` | a CAPTCHA or "verify you are human" page is blocking | Ostler never solves or evades these. Run with `--headed`, complete it in the window, then the agent calls `wait_for_human`. A persistent `--profile-dir` with a logged-in session triggers fewer challenges |
| `browser exited before DevTools was ready (is another Ostler or Chrome already using profile …)` | Chrome allows one process per profile and two servers (two agent windows, subagents) share one `--profile-dir` | give each server its own `--profile-dir`, or omit it (throwaway profile per server; any number can run at once) |
| Google, DuckDuckGo or Bing return a wall or no results | search engines challenge headless browsers; Ostler is built for forms and does not evade these | use your agent's own search tool for search and Ostler for the target site. If you must search through Ostler, run one `--headed` server with its own `--profile-dir` and solve the check yourself |
| A site blocks the browser or shows a CAPTCHA | automation detection | Ostler does not evade it; see [Searching the web](#searching-the-web) |
| Rebuilt `ostler` but the agent still behaves as before | the client keeps the old server process | reconnect the MCP client (Claude Code: `/mcp`; others: restart it) |

## When not to use Ostler

Ostler is a form-filling browser for an agent working on your behalf, on one machine. It is the wrong tool when:

- **The site walls off automation.** CAPTCHA, Cloudflare/Turnstile, "verify you are human" pages and search-engine bot checks are reported with a `CHALLENGE:` line and handed to a person. Ostler never solves or bypasses them, and it is not built to avoid detection: there is no stealth patching, fingerprint spoofing, residential proxy or IP rotation. A site that blocks headless or datacenter Chrome will block Ostler. `--headed` plus a persistent `--profile-dir` lets *you* pass a check once; it does not make a bot wall go away.
- **You need scale.** Each server drives one local Chrome (tabs share its cookies and profile). It is not a remote or cloud browser farm, not a crawler, and not meant for bulk scraping or high-volume account creation. More sessions means more servers, each with its own profile and its own memory use (see [Benchmarks](https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/docs/benchmarks.html)).
- **The flow needs an identity Ostler does not have.** There is no mailbox, phone number, SMS/OTP receiver or authenticator: one-time codes, email-link verification, passkeys, hardware keys and 2FA prompts need a person. Passwords and card numbers are never read back or remembered; sensitive fields are refused and the agent is told to ask you. It does not create accounts on your behalf out of thin air.
- **The page is outside what the injected runtime can see.** Cross-origin iframes (many hosted card fields), closed shadow roots, canvas-drawn UIs, native OS dialogs and file pickers, and desktop apps are not reachable. A control that stays disabled until a person scrolls or hovers is reported as disabled rather than worked around.
- **A wrong submit is expensive and nobody is checking.** Ostler verifies every value by reading it back and refuses to call a submit a success without evidence, but it cannot know whether a form means what it says. For payments, legal acceptance and anything irreversible, run with `--require-confirm-submit` and review the result yourself.

When Ostler cannot finish, it says which field and why (rejected value with the page's own message, hidden or disabled control, key not found) and points at `screenshot` for the element; it does not report a partial fill as done.

## Searching the web

Ostler drives a real Chrome, but from a fresh, headless session many sites treat it as a bot. What to expect (it varies by network and over time):

- **Google, DuckDuckGo, Brave, Startpage, Reddit, news sites such as the NYT:** often a bot wall or CAPTCHA. Ostler reports it and hands off to a person; it never tries to solve or get around it.
- **Bing:** usually loads (but it may ignore `first=` / "Page 2" and serve page 1 again to a headless session), but may return results unrelated to your query ("Some results have been removed"). When a search-results URL's visible text matches fewer than about half of the query's words, `navigate` adds `Warning: results do not seem to match the query "..."`. Treat the results as unreliable and try another engine or `--headed`.

What helps, honestly:

1. Run `--headed` with a persistent `--profile-dir`, one profile per server (Chrome locks a profile while it is in use). A person clears a CAPTCHA or signs in once in the visible window; cookies persist for later runs.
2. When the agent hits a wall it calls `wait_for_human`: it pauses, you solve the page in the window, and it resumes from the same page.
3. For pure discovery (finding which pages to read), use a search API; it is more reliable than scraping a results page. Ostler is best at reading the pages you already have URLs for and at filling forms.

Do not spoof the user agent or try to hide automation; it is unreliable and not something Ostler supports.

If it still fails, open an issue with the output of `ostler doctor` and your OS and Chrome version.
